questions.q: Many farming peoples of eastern North America grew a trio of crops that supported one another in the same fields. Which crops made up this group?
options: Wheat, barley, and oats
Rice, cotton, and indigo
Maize, beans, and squash
Potatoes, flax, and hemp
questions.explain: Maize gave beans a pole to climb, beans enriched the soil, and squash shaded out weeds, a system known as the Three Sisters.

questions.q: Which nations formed the original Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, a league that coordinated peace and decision-making among its members?
options: Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole
Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca
Pequot, Narragansett, Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Abenaki
Powhatan, Pamunkey, Mattaponi, Nansemond, and Chickahominy
questions.explain: The Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee joined in a league of peace centered in what is now New York; the Tuscarora joined later, in the 1700s.

questions.q: In Haudenosaunee society, clan mothers held the authority to name and, if necessary, remove the League's chiefs. This role reflects which feature of the society?
options: Rulers were chosen only from the oldest sons of chiefs
Priests controlled all political appointments
Women were barred from any public decision-making
Descent and property were traced through the mother's line
questions.explain: Matrilineal clans gave women important political and economic influence, a contrast to the male-dominated governance of European colonizers.

questions.q: Which region was home to Native peoples who built multistory adobe dwellings and used irrigation to farm in a dry climate?
options: The Southwest
The Pacific Northwest
The Great Plains
The Northeast woodlands
questions.explain: Ancestral Pueblo peoples and their descendants adapted corn farming to the arid Southwest with irrigation and compact, multistory adobe villages.

questions.q: The Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest could support large, settled populations without farming mainly because of which resource?
options: Vast herds of bison on open grasslands
Abundant salmon and other fish and sea life
Irrigated fields of maize and beans
Large imports of grain from the Southwest
questions.explain: Rich salmon runs, shellfish, and forests let Northwest societies build permanent villages, trade networks, and elaborate art without agriculture.

questions.q: The potlatch of Northwest Coast peoples is best described as which of the following?
options: A ceremonial feast in which hosts gave away wealth to confirm status
A council in which neighboring nations signed treaties of peace
A harvest festival held to honor the spirit of the corn crop
A trading fair in which families exchanged goods for coins
questions.explain: Hosts demonstrated rank and generosity by distributing goods to guests, who by attending witnessed and validated the host's claims.

questions.q: Before European contact, Native peoples of the Great Plains mostly relied on which animal for food and materials?
options: Cattle
Elk
Sheep
Bison
questions.explain: Plains groups hunted bison on foot before horses arrived, and they used the meat, hides, and bones for food, shelter, and tools.

questions.q: Cahokia, a large city of the Mississippian culture near present-day St. Louis, was notable for which of the following?
options: Stone cathedrals and bell towers built under Spanish direction
Walled forts and trading posts erected by French fur traders
Huge earthen mounds and a dense population of farmers and craft workers
A network of canals linking the settlement to the Pacific
questions.explain: Cahokia peaked around 1050 to 1150 CE, and its mounds, including Monks Mound, show a complex society with hierarchy and long-distance trade.

questions.q: The Hohokam of present-day Arizona are known for which achievement in adapting to their environment?
options: Building extensive networks of irrigation canals in the desert
Constructing earthen burial mounds along the Ohio River
Domesticating the horse for long-distance trade
Developing a written alphabet for recording harvests
questions.explain: The Hohokam dug hundreds of miles of canals from rivers to water crops of maize, beans, squash, and cotton in the Sonoran Desert.

questions.q: According to the most widely accepted scholarly account taught in US history courses, the ancestors of Native Americans first entered the Americas by way of which route?
options: A coastal voyage by skin boat from Polynesia across the open Pacific during the last Ice Age
A northern sea route first opened by Viking explorers
A land bridge, Beringia, linking Asia and North America during the last Ice Age
A land connection across the Atlantic from northern Europe
questions.explain: Beringia was exposed when sea levels were low, and later migrants spread south, adapting to many environments; scholars also discuss coastal routes.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why Native Americans of the Northeast sometimes burned underbrush in forests?
options: It was required by treaties that Native nations had signed with early colonial governments
It prevented the spread of diseases brought by Europeans
It cleared large spaces for cattle ranches and pastures
It created open land that encouraged game animals and made hunting and travel easier
questions.explain: Controlled burning altered ecosystems and showed that Native peoples actively managed the environment well before Europeans arrived.

questions.q: Many Native societies understood land as something groups used and shared, while English colonists generally saw it as something that could be privately owned and sold. What was a likely result of these differing views?
options: Quick agreement on fixed property lines recognized by both sides
Misunderstandings over what treaties and land transactions actually meant
Peaceful elimination of every dispute over land claims
A shared legal system for recording and defending land titles
questions.explain: Each side often thought it was agreeing to something different, since Native signers might grant shared use rights while colonists believed they had purchased land outright.

questions.q: Which item served as an important trade and diplomatic good among Native peoples of the Northeast, often made from shells?
options: Pemmican
Tallow
Wampum
Calumet
questions.explain: Wampum belts and strings of shell beads recorded agreements and sealed alliances, and the Dutch and English later adapted them for trade.

questions.q: The Aztec (Mexica) capital of Tenochtitlan was built on an island in which lake?
options: Lake Titicaca
Lake Texcoco
Lake Champlain
Lake Superior
questions.explain: Tenochtitlan stood on Lake Texcoco, linked to the shore by causeways, and Mexico City now occupies the site.

questions.q: Which empire, centered in the Andes with its capital at Cuzco, was conquered by a small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro in the 1530s?
options: The Inca Empire
The Maya city-states
The Aztec Empire
The Mississippian chiefdoms
questions.explain: Pizarro exploited a civil war and smallpox among the Inca, whose empire stretched along the Andes, to seize control by 1533.

questions.q: The Maya civilization of Mesoamerica is best known for which of these achievements?
options: A road network that carried horse-drawn wagons
Iron tools that supported large-scale mining
Printing of books on movable type
A written language and advanced astronomy and mathematics
questions.explain: The Maya developed hieroglyphic writing, a sophisticated calendar, and the concept of zero, centuries before Columbus.

questions.q: Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico was a center of which people?
options: Hopewell
Powhatan
Ancestral Pueblo
Lakota
questions.explain: Chaco's great houses and roads show a complex Ancestral Pueblo society that flourished for more than three centuries beginning in the mid-800s CE.

questions.q: Which Native group lived in a Far North environment and relied heavily on hunting sea mammals such as seals and whales?
options: The Hohokam
The Inuit
The Pequot
The Powhatan
questions.explain: In the Arctic, farming was impossible, so the Inuit built a way of life around marine hunting, sledges, and kayaks.

questions.q: Before European contact, many Native peoples in California gathered acorns as a staple food. This indicates that their societies were most likely supported by what?
options: Gathering, fishing, and hunting in a region of rich natural resources
Large-scale plow agriculture using oxen and iron tools
Herding livestock across wide pastures year-round
Trading for imported grain from distant European merchants
questions.explain: California's mild climate and varied food sources supported dense populations and many languages without widespread farming.

questions.q: By the early 1600s, the Powhatan Confederacy in coastal Virginia was led by Wahunsenacawh. How was it organized?
options: As a league of five equal nations governed by clan mothers
As scattered independent bands that had no central leader
As a loose set of independent bands that met only once a year and had no central leader
As a paramount chiefdom of about thirty groups that paid tribute to one leader
questions.explain: Wahunsenacawh, called Powhatan by the English, built a powerful chiefdom of Algonquian-speaking groups in the Tidewater region.

questions.q: Which language family included many peoples of New England and the Chesapeake, such as the Wampanoag and Powhatan, who met English colonists?
options: Algonquian
Iroquoian
Siouan
Uto-Aztecan
questions.explain: Algonquian-speaking nations lived across much of the Atlantic coast, where early English settlements took shape.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Native American trade before 1492?
options: Trade was limited to occasional exchanges of food between a few neighboring villages in each region
It depended entirely on goods brought by European merchants
Long-distance exchange moved goods such as copper, shells, and obsidian across the continent
Most tribal governments banned it to protect local crafts
questions.explain: Archaeological finds of Great Lakes copper and Gulf Coast shells far from their sources show wide networks of exchange.

questions.q: A Native farmer in the Eastern Woodlands might have planted corn in mounded hills with beans growing up the stalks. This practice is evidence of what?
options: Dependence on iron plows and draft animals from Europe
Absence of any settled villages or permanent fields
Reliance on tools introduced by Spanish traders
Sophisticated agricultural knowledge adapted to local conditions
questions.explain: Native farmers developed efficient, sustainable planting methods long before contact, and farming provided much of their diet.

questions.q: Which statement most accurately describes Native American societies in 1491?
options: They shared a single language, religion, and government that stretched across all of North America
They were diverse, with hundreds of languages and many forms of government and economy
They lived mainly in small, isolated family groups without villages
They practiced no agriculture anywhere on the continent
questions.explain: Native societies ranged from mobile hunters to large agricultural states and chiefdoms, with great variety in religion and politics.

questions.q: The Adena and Hopewell cultures, which preceded Mississippian societies, are best known for building what?
options: Earthen burial and ceremonial mounds in the Ohio River valley
Cliff dwellings in the Southwest
Large ocean-going canoes in the Pacific Northwest
Stone pyramids in central Mexico
questions.explain: These mound-building cultures traded widely and left earthworks across the Ohio Valley, visible long after their builders' societies changed.

questions.q: Which crop, domesticated in Mesoamerica, became the foundation of agriculture for many peoples across the Americas?
options: Wheat
Sugarcane
Rice
Maize
questions.explain: Domesticated from a wild grass in what is now Mexico, maize spread north and south and supported population growth.

questions.q: A Native elder in the Southwest explains that her people emerged from the earth and have always lived on their land. This explanation best illustrates which idea?
options: The use of written scripture preserved on paper
A legal claim formally recognized by the Spanish crown
Oral traditions as a form of historical and spiritual knowledge
Evidence of a recent migration from Europe
questions.explain: Many Native nations preserved history and religious belief through oral tradition, which often ties people closely to particular places.

questions.q: Why did early European arrivals often find eastern North America to be heavily populated rather than empty wilderness?
options: Spanish settlers had already filled most of the interior with towns, missions, and cattle ranches
Native peoples had farmed, settled villages, and managed the land for centuries
The region had been left uninhabited since the last Ice Age
Native peoples lived only on a few islands off the coast
questions.explain: Eastern landscapes reflected centuries of farming, burning, and village life, though epidemics soon reduced many communities.

questions.q: Which Native group became known for adopting the horse and shifting to a mobile bison-hunting life on the Plains after Spanish colonization?
options: The Mohawk
The Powhatan
The Chumash
The Comanche
questions.explain: Horses obtained from Spanish New Mexico transformed Plains life, and the Comanche became powerful traders and warriors.

questions.q: Which feature distinguished the Haudenosaunee League's governing council, which met at Onondaga?
options: Decisions were reached by consensus among representatives of the member nations
The council voted by simple majority rule among all adult citizens of the member nations
A single hereditary king ruled over all the member nations
Decrees were issued by a monarch living across the ocean
questions.explain: Council debate aimed at unanimity, and the League's structure has long fascinated scholars of political history.

questions.q: The Great Basin and the Southwest differ from the Northwest Coast in what respect before 1500?
options: They had far larger populations because dependable ocean fishing supplied food in every season of the year
Peoples there faced scarcer resources and adapted with smaller, more mobile or irrigation-based communities
They enjoyed heavy rainfall and dense coastal forests
They produced the main exports of the Atlantic trade
questions.explain: Dry lands demanded different strategies such as seed gathering, small hunting bands, or irrigated farming.

questions.q: Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage was financed by the monarchs of which kingdom?
options: Portugal
England
Spain
France
questions.explain: Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile and Aragon backed his plan to reach Asia by sailing west, after Portugal had declined it.

questions.q: What was Columbus's main goal when he sailed west across the Atlantic in 1492?
options: To find a new route to the trade riches of Asia
To found a colony for religious dissenters
To discover a continent unknown to Europeans
To spread Protestant teachings
questions.explain: Europeans wanted direct access to Asian spices and silks, and Columbus believed a westward route would be shorter than going around Africa.

questions.q: Columbus's first landfall in the Americas in 1492 was in which area?
options: Newfoundland
The coast of Florida
The Bahamas
The Yucatan Peninsula
questions.explain: He reached an island in the Bahamas, then explored Cuba and Hispaniola, believing he was near Asia.

questions.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) was an agreement that did what?
options: Ended a long religious war between Spain and England
Granted Native peoples protection under Spanish royal law
Allowed France to settle North America
Divided newly claimed lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal
questions.explain: Brokered with the help of the pope, it set a north-south line in the Atlantic, with Spain claiming lands to the west and Portugal to the east.

questions.q: The Columbian Exchange refers to the transfer of which of the following between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres?
options: Only gold and silver mined by Native workers
Plants, animals, diseases, and people
Only European religious ideas and church customs
Only enslaved laborers brought from West Africa
questions.explain: The movement of crops, livestock, germs, and peoples after 1492 reshaped life on every continent.

questions.q: Which pair of items traveled from the Americas to Europe in the Columbian Exchange?
options: Horses and wheat
Cattle and sugarcane
Potatoes and tomatoes
Pigs and grapes
questions.explain: New World crops like potatoes, tomatoes, and maize transformed European diets, and potatoes in particular helped populations grow.

questions.q: Which pair of animals brought by Europeans changed Native life in the Americas?
options: Bison and turkeys
Horses and cattle
Llamas and alpacas
Rabbits and parrots
questions.explain: Horses transformed mobility, hunting, and warfare, while cattle and pigs reshaped landscapes; none of these species lived in the Americas before 1492.

questions.q: What was the single greatest cause of the huge decline in Native American populations after 1492?
options: Famine caused by climate change
Battles between Native nations
Voluntary migration to Europe
Epidemic diseases such as smallpox
questions.explain: Native peoples lacked immunity to diseases like smallpox, measles, and influenza, which killed enormous numbers, often before sustained European contact.

questions.q: Why did Old World diseases spread so lethally among Native peoples in the Americas?
options: Populations had no prior exposure and so lacked immunity
Natives had weaker bodies than Europeans
Spanish doctors spread disease on purpose as a policy
Diseases came only from imported animals
questions.explain: Isolated for thousands of years, Native populations were 'virgin soil' for pathogens common in Eurasia and Africa, so outbreaks could be devastating.

questions.q: Prince Henry of Portugal, sometimes called 'the Navigator,' is best known for what?
options: Leading the first Atlantic crossing to North America
Founding the first Protestant church in Portugal
Conquering the Aztec Empire in Mexico on behalf of the Portuguese crown
Sponsoring Portuguese voyages of exploration down the coast of Africa
questions.explain: Voyages Henry sponsored in the 1400s pushed down the African coast and laid groundwork for routes to Asia. The famed "school" at Sagres is now regarded by historians as largely a legend.

questions.q: Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1497 to 1499 was significant because he did what?
options: Reached the Pacific from the Americas
Landed in the Caribbean
Sailed around Africa to reach India
Sailed around the globe
questions.explain: His success gave Portugal a direct sea route to Asian trade, bypassing Mediterranean middlemen and Muslim and Venetian merchants.

questions.q: Which ship type, small and maneuverable with triangular sails, was favored by Portuguese and Spanish explorers?
options: The caravel
The galleon
The clipper
The longship
questions.explain: The caravel could sail well against the wind, which allowed ocean exploration along unfamiliar coasts.

questions.q: Which technological advances helped European sailors cross the open ocean in the late 1400s?
options: Steam engines and iron hulls for ocean-going ships
The compass, the astrolabe, and improved ship designs
Radar and accurate chronometers for plotting position
Telescopes and printing presses, and nothing else
questions.explain: Navigation tools and sturdier ships let sailors find their position and return home, making oceanic voyages less risky.

questions.q: The Waldseemuller map of 1507 is famous for being the first to do what?
options: Use the name 'America' for the New World
Show the Pacific Ocean in detail
Mark the location of Jamestown
Draw the borders of the Thirteen Colonies
questions.explain: The map's creators honored Amerigo Vespucci, who argued that the lands were a separate continent; the Library of Congress holds the surviving copy.

questions.q: Who led the Spanish expedition whose members completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1519 to 1522?
options: Hernan Cortes
Juan Ponce de Leon
Ferdinand Magellan
Amerigo Vespucci
questions.explain: Magellan died in the Philippines, but one ship under Juan Sebastian Elcano returned to Spain after circling the globe.

questions.q: Who explored the coast of Newfoundland in 1497 on behalf of England?
options: Giovanni da Verrazzano
Henry Hudson
Samuel de Champlain
John Cabot
questions.explain: Cabot's voyage under Henry VII was the basis for later English claims in North America.

questions.q: Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s. His voyages helped establish a claim for which country?
options: Spain
France
The Netherlands
Portugal
questions.explain: Cartier's expeditions gave France a claim to the St. Lawrence valley, where New France later developed.

questions.q: Which Spanish explorer led the conquest of the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521?
options: Francisco Pizarro
Hernan Cortes
Hernando de Soto
Francisco Vasquez de Coronado
questions.explain: With a few hundred soldiers, Cortes allied with Native enemies of the Aztecs and benefited from a smallpox epidemic.

questions.q: Which factors contributed most to the Spanish defeat of the Aztec Empire?
options: The complete absence of any organized military force among the Aztec rulers
A promise of military help from the Portuguese crown
Active cooperation from the Inca against the Aztecs
Native allies who resented Aztec rule, smallpox, and Spanish weapons
questions.explain: Peoples such as the Tlaxcalans joined Cortes against Aztec tribute demands, and epidemic disease weakened Tenochtitlan.

questions.q: Hernando de Soto's expedition in the early 1540s is notable because it did what?
options: Founded St. Augustine on the coast of Florida
Explored the St. Lawrence valley for the French crown
Traveled through the Southeast and reached the Mississippi River
Reached the Pacific coast of present-day California
questions.explain: De Soto's march across the Southeast brought violence and disease to Native communities, and he died in 1542 near the Mississippi.

questions.q: Francisco Vasquez de Coronado led an expedition in 1540 searching for what?
options: Cities of gold in the Southwest
A water route to the Pacific through Canada
A French fort on the Gulf
The Fountain of Youth
questions.explain: He found Pueblo towns instead of golden cities, and his expedition ranged as far as present-day Kansas.

questions.q: Juan Ponce de Leon is best known for which of the following?
options: Landing on the coast of Florida in 1513
Founding the first English colony
Exploring the Mississippi River
Reaching China by sea
questions.explain: Ponce de Leon named Florida and made contact there; permanent Spanish settlement came decades later at St. Augustine.

questions.q: St. Augustine, founded by Spain in 1565, is notable as what?
options: The first permanent English colony, founded by merchants to compete with Spanish claims in the region
The capital of the French colony of New France
The first Dutch trading post on the Hudson River
The oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the continental United States
questions.explain: Pedro Menendez de Aviles established it to protect Spanish treasure fleets and drive out a French Huguenot outpost nearby.

questions.q: Why did Spain establish St. Augustine in 1565?
options: To search for gold and silver deposits in the Appalachian Mountains for the Spanish crown
To house English prisoners captured by Spanish ships
To secure Florida against French Protestant settlement and protect shipping routes
To serve as a base for the slave trade to Africa
questions.explain: Spanish leaders feared that a French base at Fort Caroline would threaten treasure fleets in the Florida straits, so they destroyed it.

questions.q: The encomienda system in Spanish America gave colonists the right to do what?
options: Own land outright after seven years of residence, then sell it freely to any buyer without paying duties to Spain
Receive labor and tribute from Native communities in return for nominal protection and religious instruction
Vote for representatives in colonial assemblies
Trade freely with other European powers and their colonies
questions.explain: In practice, encomienda often meant forced labor and abuse, which contributed to catastrophic population loss.

questions.q: Bartolome de las Casas is known for what role in Spanish colonial history?
options: Criticizing the mistreatment of Native peoples and urging reform
Leading the first Spanish conquest of Mexico
Founding the Jesuit order in the 1530s
Establishing the first printing press in the Americas
questions.explain: A former encomendero who became a Dominican friar, Las Casas campaigned for Native rights, helping inspire the New Laws of 1542.

questions.q: Spanish colonial society in the Americas was marked by a social hierarchy based largely on what?
options: Wealth alone, regardless of birth, ancestry, or place of residence
Level of education and ownership of books
Membership in a political party or faction
Birthplace and ancestry, with Spain-born elites at the top
questions.explain: People born in Spain held the highest rank, followed by American-born Spaniards, mixed-ancestry groups, and then Native and African people.

questions.q: A person of mixed Spanish and Native American ancestry in colonial Spanish America was called a what?
options: Creole
Mestizo
Peninsulare
Conquistador
questions.explain: Mestizos formed a large part of Spanish colonial society, reflecting extensive intermarriage, often under unequal conditions.

questions.q: The silver mines of Potosi and Zacatecas were important because they did what?
options: Provided the main source of income for Native communities
Replaced the need for farming in Spain's villages
Gave Spain enormous wealth and tied the global economy together
Ended the encomienda system across the empire
questions.explain: Silver from Spanish America flowed to Europe and Asia, financing Spanish power and fueling price inflation across Europe.

questions.q: How did the flow of New World silver and gold affect Europe in the 1500s?
options: It collapsed trade in the major Atlantic ports of Europe
It made most European currencies worthless overnight
It ended the need for banks in European cities
It contributed to inflation and increased Spain's power
questions.explain: As more precious metal circulated, prices rose across Europe, a development historians call the Price Revolution.

questions.q: Which concept best describes the idea that a nation's strength rests on accumulating gold and silver and maintaining favorable trade?
options: Feudalism
Mercantilism
Federalism
Laissez-faire
questions.explain: European powers, including Spain and England, valued colonies for raw materials and as markets that would help the home country's economy.

questions.q: Which event in 1492 completed the Spanish Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula?
options: The defeat of the Armada
The fall of Constantinople
The fall of Granada
The conquest of Mexico
questions.explain: The surrender of Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Iberia, ended Muslim rule on the peninsula, and the victorious Catholic monarchs then financed Columbus.

questions.q: Traditional accounts link the Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 to European exploration because it did what?
options: Increased Europe's interest in finding new sea routes to Asia
Opened the Mediterranean to free trade for all merchants
Ended nearly all contact between Europe and Asia
Persuaded Europeans to give up on Asian goods
questions.explain: Traditional accounts say Ottoman control of eastern routes pushed Europeans to seek sea routes to Asia, though historians note Portuguese voyages had begun before 1453.

questions.q: Which event in 1588 weakened Spain's naval dominance and encouraged English colonization?
options: The sinking of the Mayflower
The Dutch seizure of Brazil
The signing of the Treaty of Paris
The defeat of the Spanish Armada
questions.explain: England's victory over the Armada boosted English confidence and challenged Spanish control of the Atlantic.

questions.q: How did the printing press with movable type, developed in Europe around 1450, affect exploration and the Reformation?
options: It spread ideas, maps, and reports of new lands quickly
It slowed the spread of religious ideas across Europe
It made maps and sea charts unnecessary for sailors
It was banned in nearly every European country until 1600
questions.explain: Printing made books, pamphlets, and maps cheaper and more widely available, helping both explorers' accounts and Protestant ideas travel.

questions.q: Martin Luther began the Protestant Reformation in 1517 by doing what?
options: Founding a new Protestant colony in Virginia
Sailing west across the Atlantic to find a route to Asia
Publicly challenging church practices such as selling indulgences
Translating Greek texts from the Bible into Latin
questions.explain: His Ninety-five Theses criticized selling indulgences, and the printing press spread his ideas across Europe.

questions.q: John Calvin's teaching of predestination held that what?
options: Salvation could be earned by good works
God had chosen in advance who would be saved
The church had no role
All people would be saved equally
questions.explain: This idea shaped later Puritans, who sought signs that they were among the elect.

questions.q: Why did King Henry VIII break with the Roman Catholic Church in the 1530s?
options: He wanted control over the English church and an annulment of his marriage
He wished to join Martin Luther's reform movement in Germany
He was forced out of the church by Parliament's army
He wanted to send English missionaries to America
questions.explain: The Act of Supremacy (1534) made the monarch head of the Church of England, setting off long religious conflict that later drove colonization.

questions.q: Which group sought to 'purify' the Church of England of remaining Catholic practices?
options: The Quakers
The Anglicans
The Huguenots
The Puritans
questions.explain: Puritans sought reform within the Church of England, while Separatists such as the Pilgrims wanted to leave it entirely.

questions.q: French Protestants who faced persecution in France were known as what?
options: Jesuits
Huguenots
Separatists
Pietists
questions.explain: Some Huguenots tried to settle in Florida and South Carolina before Spain destroyed Fort Caroline.

questions.q: Which approach best describes the French colonial effort in North America?
options: Large agricultural colonies filled with families who farmed the land for generations
Dense urban centers built around rich silver mines
Small settlements focused on fur trading and alliances with Native nations
Plantation colonies worked by enslaved Africans
questions.explain: French traders relied on Native partners for furs, so New France stayed thinly settled compared to the English colonies.

questions.q: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. What was one reason France wanted it?
options: To establish a haven for persecuted French Catholics
To grow tobacco for sale in European markets
To mine silver and send it back to Paris
To control the fur trade along the St. Lawrence River
questions.explain: Quebec served as a trading post where Native hunters exchanged furs for European goods, linking France to a vast Native trade network.

questions.q: The Dutch West India Company established New Netherland to pursue what goal?
options: Religious freedom for Dutch Calvinists
Acquiring land for a royal colony
Profit from the fur trade and commerce
Conversion of Native peoples
questions.explain: The company wanted trade profits, and the settlement at New Amsterdam grew into a commercial hub with diverse inhabitants.

questions.q: How did Spanish missions, such as those in Florida and New Mexico, aim to change Native communities?
options: By converting Native peoples to Catholicism and having them labor for the colony
By granting Native nations permanent seats in colonial assemblies and giving them votes
By paying Native communities to leave the region peacefully
By teaching them Protestant doctrines and English law
questions.explain: Missions combined religious teaching with demands for labor and tribute, which many Native peoples resisted.

questions.q: Spanish settlers in New Mexico, beginning with Juan de Onate's expedition in 1598, set up ranches and missions where what resource was central to the economy?
options: Wage labor from European migrants
Native labor and tribute
Fur trading
Slave plantations producing tobacco
questions.explain: Onate demanded labor and food from Pueblo communities, which stoked resentment that later exploded in the Pueblo Revolt.

questions.q: Sir Walter Raleigh sponsored the English colony at which location in the 1580s?
options: Roanoke Island
Plymouth
Jamestown
Boston
questions.explain: Raleigh's colonists, who landed off the coast of present-day North Carolina, vanished by 1590, leaving the word CROATOAN carved on a post.

questions.q: What became of the Roanoke colonists left on the island in 1587?
options: They were captured by the Spanish and taken to Florida
They sailed back to England on a passing supply ship and settled near Plymouth after the voyage
They were all killed in a massacre recorded by the English
They disappeared, leaving no confirmed explanation, by the time supply ships returned in 1590
questions.explain: The fate of the "Lost Colony" remains debated; some scholars suggest survivors joined neighboring Native communities.

questions.q: Which factor made England's early colonization attempts, such as Roanoke, more difficult?
options: A ban on colonization issued by Parliament after Raleigh lost the queen's favor
Limited funding and the need for supplies across a long ocean voyage
Native control of every Atlantic harbor
Fear of a Dutch invasion and nothing more
questions.explain: Early private ventures lacked enough capital and support, which is one reason England turned to joint-stock companies.

questions.q: The joint-stock company, used to finance English colonies like Jamestown, worked by doing what?
options: Having the king pay all costs
Limiting investment to nobles
Pooling money from many investors to share risks and profits
Relying on voluntary contributions from Parliament
questions.explain: Investors bought shares in a venture, spreading the financial risk of expensive and uncertain colonization.

questions.q: Sir Humphrey Gilbert, Raleigh's half-brother, is known for what role in English colonization?
options: Claiming Newfoundland for England in 1583 and promoting colonization
Leading the first English settlement in Virginia in 1607
Establishing Plymouth Colony
Negotiating the Treaty of Tordesillas
questions.explain: Gilbert's efforts, though unsuccessful, helped set a model of private colonization authorized by a royal patent.

questions.q: Which of these best summarizes the Protestant Reformation's role in the colonization of North America?
options: It persuaded nearly all Europeans to stay home and abandon overseas ventures after 1520
It ended competition among European powers for good
It led Spain to adopt Protestantism and welcome refugees
Religious conflict motivated some groups to seek new homes and made Protestant England a rival of Spain
questions.explain: The break from Rome created religious rivalries that influenced English colonial goals and drove groups such as Puritans and Pilgrims to the Atlantic.

questions.q: Before the Atlantic slave trade grew, Portuguese traders began transporting enslaved Africans to which places to work on sugar plantations?
options: The upper Mississippi River valley in North America
Farmlands in northern France and the Low Countries
Atlantic islands such as Madeira and Sao Tome
The French settlements around Quebec in Canada
questions.explain: Portugal developed sugar plantations on Atlantic islands using enslaved African labor, a model later extended to the Americas.

questions.q: Which crop drove the early demand for enslaved African labor in the Caribbean and Brazil?
options: Wheat
Sugar
Tobacco
Cotton
questions.explain: Sugar was labor-intensive and very profitable, and plantation owners turned to enslaved Africans as Native workers died in large numbers.

questions.q: Why did European colonists in the Caribbean turn increasingly to enslaved Africans in the 1500s and 1600s?
options: Africans had asked European traders to carry them to the Americas
Native populations had been sharply reduced and demand for plantation labor was rising
Native Americans had all converted to Christianity and left the plantations
New royal laws required the use of African workers
questions.explain: Disease and harsh conditions devastated Native workers, so planters looked to the transatlantic slave trade for a larger labor supply.

questions.q: The forced voyage of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic is known as what?
options: The Great Migration
The Trail of Tears
The Columbian Exchange
The Middle Passage
questions.explain: Millions of people were packed aboard ships in terrible conditions, and many died during the crossing.

questions.q: The West African kingdom of Mali, whose ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage in 1324, grew rich mainly through what?
options: Atlantic trade in sugar
Plantation agriculture exports
Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt
Silver mining
questions.explain: Control of gold trade routes across the Sahara made Mali wealthy, and Timbuktu became a center of learning and commerce.

questions.q: Which West African kingdom, led by King Afonso I (early 1500s), converted to Christianity and tried to limit the slave trade's abuses through correspondence with Portugal?
options: Kongo
Songhai
Benin
Ghana
questions.explain: Afonso I complained to the Portuguese king about slave raiding that depopulated his kingdom.

questions.q: How did slavery in West Africa before European contact differ from the later Atlantic system?
options: African slavery varied in form and was not usually race-based hereditary chattel slavery on plantations
Slavery was entirely unknown anywhere in West Africa until European ships arrived on the coast in the 1400s
African captives were always freed after seven years of work
The Atlantic system was much smaller than African slavery
questions.explain: Forms of bondage existed in Africa, but European demand created a far larger trade and a system based on race and perpetual, inheritable status.

questions.q: In Spanish America, the first enslaved Africans were brought mainly to do what?
options: Serve as soldiers against Native peoples in frontier wars
Settle land as free farmers under royal protection
Operate Spanish trading ships between Seville and Havana
Work in mines and on plantations after Native populations declined
questions.explain: Enslaved Africans were put to forced labor in mining, agriculture, and domestic service across the Caribbean and mainland.

questions.q: The Spanish term 'conquistador' refers to what?
options: A priest who ran a mission among Native communities
A colonial tax collector working for the crown
A Spanish soldier-adventurer who conquered Native lands
A Native ally who fought alongside Spain
questions.explain: Conquistadors like Cortes and Pizarro led private expeditions licensed by the crown and shared in the spoils.

questions.q: What was the Spanish crown's main motive in granting conquistadors the right to explore and settle lands?
options: To establish representative governments in the colonies
To gain wealth, expand its empire, and spread Catholicism
To promote freedom of religion for all subjects
To limit colonial trade and keep settlements small
questions.explain: Often summarized as 'God, gold, and glory,' these goals drove Spanish expansion in the Americas.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the long-term effect of the Columbian Exchange on the Americas?
options: It left the environment and Native societies unchanged because contact was brief and minor
It transformed ecosystems and societies through new species and diseases
It stopped most migration across the Atlantic Ocean
It made Native societies richer and healthier
questions.explain: Livestock, new crops, and diseases altered landscapes, diets, and populations, effects that continued for centuries.

questions.q: Giovanni da Verrazzano explored the Atlantic coast of North America in 1524 and sailed on behalf of which country?
options: Spain
England
France
The Netherlands
questions.explain: His voyage contributed to French claims along the Atlantic coast, including the New York harbor area.

questions.q: The Spanish colonial system of missions, presidios, and pueblos was designed mainly to do what?
options: Create independent colonial republics ruled by settlers
Encourage Native peoples to govern their own communities
Open trade with France and the Dutch Republic
Secure and settle frontier lands under Spanish control
questions.explain: Missions converted Native peoples, presidios were military forts, and pueblos were civilian towns, together extending Spain's power.

questions.q: Why did Spanish religious orders such as the Franciscans and Dominicans accompany colonizers?
options: To convert Native peoples to Catholicism
To serve as colonial governors
To collect tariffs
To record maps of the Atlantic coast
questions.explain: Spain's claim to the Americas rested partly on a mission to spread Christianity, though missionaries sometimes clashed with settlers over Native treatment.

questions.q: The 1550-1551 debate at Valladolid, Spain, between Las Casas and Juan Gines de Sepulveda concerned what question?
options: How Native peoples should be treated and whether conquest was justified
Whether Spain should abandon its colonies in the Americas
Whether to build a canal across the Isthmus of Panama
Whether Spain should join the Protestant Reformation
questions.explain: Las Casas argued Native peoples had rational souls and rights, while Sepulveda defended Spanish conquest; the crown did not settle the matter decisively.

questions.q: By the late 1500s, which factor most encouraged England to challenge Spain in the Atlantic?
options: A recent treaty of alliance between England and Portugal against the Spanish king
Spain's wealth from the Americas and England's rivalry with Catholic Spain
Pressure from the pope to colonize the Americas
An alliance between England and the Aztecs
questions.explain: Privateers like Francis Drake raided Spanish ships, and the rivalry shaped English interest in claiming land of their own.

questions.q: Among the historical paintings in the Capitol Rotunda is one titled 'Landing of Columbus.' Which event does it depict?
options: Columbus's return to Spain in 1493 with captive Taino
The founding of Jamestown by the Virginia Company
Columbus's arrival in the Caribbean in 1492
Columbus's death in Valladolid in 1506
questions.explain: John Vanderlyn's painting, installed in 1847, shows the Spanish party arriving on shore in 1492 while Native people watch.

questions.q: The Capitol Rotunda contains a painting called 'Embarkation of the Pilgrims.' Whose departure for America does it commemorate?
options: The Catholics who left Spain for Maryland in 1634
The Puritans who sailed to Boston in 1630
The Huguenots who left France for Florida
The Separatists who left Delfshaven for Plymouth in 1620
questions.explain: Robert Weir's painting depicts the Pilgrims' departure from Holland, where they had lived after leaving England for religious reasons.

questions.q: Which expedition leader appears in the Capitol Rotunda painting 'Discovery of the Mississippi'?
options: Samuel de Champlain
Robert La Salle
Christopher Columbus
Hernando de Soto
questions.explain: William Powell's painting depicts de Soto's party reaching the Mississippi River in 1541.

questions.q: The Capitol Rotunda painting 'Baptism of Pocahontas' depicts a young Powhatan woman at Jamestown. What does the event show about English colonial aims?
options: The recognition of Native land titles by English courts and the end of colonial land seizures
The spread of religious freedom among the colonists
The effort to convert Native peoples to Christianity and bind them to the colony
The end of conflict between settlers and Native groups
questions.explain: Pocahontas (Matoaka) was baptized Rebecca around 1613 while held by the English, and her 1614 marriage to John Rolfe brought a brief peace.

questions.q: A 1500s European map shows North and South America as a new landmass separate from Asia. How would this map most likely have affected European thinking?
options: It persuaded Europe's monarchs to end exploration altogether and to focus on Asian trade by land
It encouraged Europeans to see the Americas as lands to claim and explore
It made Europeans believe that Asia was much closer
It led to peace agreements with Native peoples
questions.explain: Maps that placed a distinct continent between Europe and Asia made the Americas a target for imperial claims and new expeditions.

questions.q: A Native leader in the early 1500s watches Spaniards demand gold and labor and says, 'These strangers do not understand that land cannot be owned.' His statement most clearly reflects what?
options: A difference between Native and European views of land and obligation
Native leaders' general support for Spanish rule and for the demands of colonial officials
A desire to adopt European law and customs
Fear of the Atlantic Ocean and long voyages
questions.explain: Differences over land use and ownership caused recurring conflict, though individual Native leaders held varied views.

questions.q: Which of these events came earliest?
options: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
Columbus's first voyage to the Americas
The founding of Jamestown
The Pilgrims' landing at Plymouth
questions.explain: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, followed by the Armada defeat (1588), Jamestown (1607), and Plymouth (1620).

questions.q: Which sequence of events is in correct chronological order?
options: St. Augustine founded, Roanoke settled, Cortes defeats the Aztecs
Roanoke settled, Cortes defeats the Aztecs, St. Augustine founded
Cortes defeats the Aztecs, Roanoke settled, St. Augustine founded
Cortes defeats the Aztecs, St. Augustine founded, Roanoke settled
questions.explain: The Aztec conquest occurred in 1519 to 1521, St. Augustine was founded in 1565, and the Roanoke colonies came in 1585 and 1587.

questions.q: Which of these events happened first?
options: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy
The founding of Quebec
The English defeat of the Armada
questions.explain: Luther's protest came in 1517, followed by Henry VIII's break with Rome in 1534, the Armada in 1588, and Quebec in 1608.

questions.q: What was the main reason Portugal sent ships along the African coast in the 1400s?
options: To find places for farmers to settle
To spread Protestantism
To search for an Atlantic land bridge
To find a sea route to Asian trade
questions.explain: Portuguese rulers sought gold, spices, and a way around the Mediterranean trade routes, which led them around Africa to India.

questions.q: By the early 1500s, Spain, Portugal, England, and France were all competing to do what?
options: Establish democratic governments in distant colonies
Gain wealth and power through overseas exploration and colonies
Protect Native Americans from disease and war
Split Europe into a group of small republics
questions.explain: The rise of strong monarchies with money and ambition fueled competition for overseas empires.

questions.q: How did the introduction of the horse by Spaniards change the lives of many Native peoples of the Plains and Southwest?
options: It eliminated bison hunting on the Plains
It ended trade between Native nations
It increased mobility for hunting, trade, and warfare
It forced them to give up hunting for farming
questions.explain: Horse ownership became a source of wealth and military strength, making groups like the Comanche and Lakota more mobile and powerful.

questions.q: Spanish colonial law in the 1500s, such as the New Laws of 1542, sought to do what?
options: Limit the abuses of the encomienda and protect Native people from enslavement
End all Spanish settlement across the Americas and return the colonists to their home villages
Give Native peoples political control of their homelands
Establish elected assemblies in the colonies
questions.explain: The New Laws attempted to curb colonists' power over Native labor, but colonists strongly resisted and enforcement was weak.

questions.q: What was the primary economic purpose of French trading posts in New France?
options: Mining gold for shipment to the French treasury
Selling tobacco to Spain for silver coins
Growing wheat for export to the French West Indies
Exchanging European goods for beaver furs from Native hunters
questions.explain: The beaver fur trade, valued for European hat-making, shaped French relations with Algonquian and Huron partners.

questions.q: How did the English model of colonization differ from that of France and Spain?
options: English settlers lived mainly among Native peoples without farms, in trading posts and villages
The English avoided building towns and permanent homes
English colonies typically sought permanent settlement by families who farmed the land
The English relied entirely on a system of missions
questions.explain: English colonists came in larger numbers, often seeking land, and this increased pressure on Native territory.

questions.q: Why did the dense English settlement of land lead to more conflict with Native peoples than did the sparser French presence?
options: The English refused all trade with Native peoples and kept entirely to their own towns
Farming settlers needed more land, displacing Native communities
Native nations always took the side of the French
The English had no real interest in owning land
questions.explain: French fur traders depended on Native hunters and needed forests intact, whereas English farmers needed cleared land.

questions.q: Which Native nations became key partners of the French in the fur trade of the St. Lawrence region?
options: The Huron (Wendat) and Algonquin
The Mohawk and Seneca
The Powhatan and Pamunkey
The Pueblo and Hopi
questions.explain: French traders allied with the Huron and Algonquin, drawing them into conflict with the Haudenosaunee, who traded with the Dutch and English.

questions.q: John Cabot's voyage in 1497, Champlain's in 1608, and Magellan's in 1519 share what feature?
options: They were all privately funded expeditions led and staffed by Native navigators and pilots
They all reached the Pacific coast of North America
Each was launched by a European power seeking new trade and territory
They all took place after the year 1700
questions.explain: Rulers licensed explorers hoping for riches, trade routes, and strategic advantage.

questions.q: Which was a likely consequence for Native peoples of European attempts to claim land?
options: A stronger sense of unity and shared purpose with the Europeans who had arrived
Improved health thanks to new foods and medicine
Expansion of Native farming across new lands
Disruption of communities through violence, disease, and displacement
questions.explain: European colonization brought demographic collapse and loss of land, while many Native peoples responded with resistance, trade, diplomacy, or adaptation.

questions.q: A government that licenses a company to trade and settle in a faraway land, as England did with the Virginia Company, reflects which motive?
options: Spreading democracy to the people of the colonies
Protecting Native homelands from European settlement through treaties and alliances
Ending Atlantic trade to keep the nation isolated
Expanding national wealth and power while sharing costs with private investors
questions.explain: Royal charters let private investors bear the risk while the crown claimed territory and expected economic benefits.

questions.q: Why was the printing press important to Protestant reformers like Luther?
options: It allowed their writings and German Bibles to reach many ordinary readers
It forced Catholic officials to attend Protestant services and to read the new Bibles aloud
It made all priests and ministers unnecessary overnight
It replaced the need for sermons in churches
questions.explain: Cheap print meant reformers could spread their message quickly, increasing literacy and religious debate.

questions.q: What did Separatists believe about the Church of England?
options: It should be kept exactly as it was
It was so corrupt that true believers should break away from it
It should merge with the Roman Catholic Church again
It should be led by Native American converts
questions.explain: Separatists, including those who later became the Pilgrims, were willing to defy the law by forming independent congregations.

questions.q: What was Amerigo Vespucci's major contribution to European understanding of the Americas?
options: He proved that the Atlantic Ocean was shallow
He founded the first permanent Spanish colony in the Caribbean on the island of Hispaniola
He argued the lands Columbus reached were a new continent, not Asia
He completed the first trip around the world
questions.explain: His writings convinced many Europeans that a 'New World' lay between them and Asia, and mapmakers named it after him.

questions.q: Which trading nation dominated the early European slave trade from West Africa in the 1400s and 1500s?
options: England
Portugal
The Netherlands
Sweden
questions.explain: Portuguese ships and forts along the African coast, such as Elmina (1482), made Portugal the leading slave trader of the early period.

questions.q: Where did the Portuguese build the fort of Elmina in 1482 to trade for gold and, later, enslaved people?
options: On the coast of present-day Ghana
On the coast of Brazil, south of Pernambuco
In the sultanate of Morocco, near Marrakesh
In the island of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean
questions.explain: Elmina became a key trading station on the Gold Coast and later a major point for the Atlantic slave trade.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how European demand shaped the African slave trade?
options: It ended all warfare among African kingdoms and brought a long period of peace
It made slavery less common across the continent
It reduced the role of African traders and rulers
It expanded the scale of enslavement and encouraged wars to capture people
questions.explain: European demand for enslaved labor encouraged some African states and traders to supply captives, intensifying violence and disruption.

questions.q: Which factor distinguishes the Spanish system of coerced labor, encomienda, from later plantation slavery?
options: Encomienda was a system that used only enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic by Portuguese slave traders
Encomienda was run by the French monarchy in Canada
Encomienda assigned labor and tribute from Native communities rather than owning people as property
Encomienda was an English system used in Virginia
questions.explain: Encomienda theoretically did not make Native people property, but it permitted forced labor and abuse.

questions.q: How did the Aztecs gain wealth and power before the arrival of the Spanish?
options: By demanding tribute from conquered peoples
By trading goods directly with European merchants
By building an overseas empire across the Atlantic
By raising cattle for export to distant markets
questions.explain: Resentment of Aztec tribute demands led many subject peoples to ally with the Spanish against Tenochtitlan.

questions.q: A Spanish document from 1513, the Requerimiento, was read to Native peoples to claim what?
options: An invitation to trade freely with the Spanish in return for protection and gifts
A guarantee of land rights for Native communities
Spain's authority and a demand that they accept Spanish rule and Christianity
An offer of Spanish citizenship for those who agreed
questions.explain: Often read in Spanish to people who could not understand it, the text justified conquest if they refused submission.

questions.q: Which Spanish explorer became the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean from the Americas, in 1513?
options: Hernan Cortes
Vasco Nunez de Balboa
Juan Ponce de Leon
Ferdinand Magellan
questions.explain: Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama and sighted the Pacific, showing that a large ocean lay between the Americas and Asia.

questions.q: By the early 1600s, which European nation's colonies were mostly concentrated in the Caribbean, Mexico, Peru, and Florida?
options: England
France
Sweden
Spain
questions.explain: Spain's American empire centered on regions with Native populations and precious metals.

questions.q: How did tobacco, a Native American crop, affect Europe after 1492?
options: It was banned by nearly all European monarchs after doctors linked it to serious illness
It was used only in Spain and never spread elsewhere
It became a widely used and traded commodity that later drove colonial economies
It stopped the spread of epidemic disease
questions.explain: Smoking spread through Europe, and tobacco became the cash crop of Virginia and Maryland.

questions.q: Which statement is the most accurate summary of the Native American response to European arrival?
options: Responses varied, including alliance, trade, resistance, and adaptation
All Native nations immediately welcomed the Europeans and shared their land without conflict
All Native nations fought Europeans from the first day
Native peoples ignored the newcomers completely
questions.explain: Nations pursued their own interests, forming alliances with Europeans, trading, or resisting depending on circumstances.

questions.q: The Counter-Reformation led Catholic Spain and France to emphasize what in their colonies?
options: Protestant reforms of the church in the colonies
Missionary work to spread Catholicism
Ending the work of religious orders overseas
Religious toleration for all faiths
questions.explain: Catholic orders such as the Jesuits and Franciscans carried out missions, linking religion with empire.

questions.q: Mercator's 1569 map projection was important for sailors because it did what?
options: Showed lines of constant compass direction as straight lines
Replaced the need for compasses on ocean voyages
Showed the territories of Native nations in detail
Showed accurate land sizes near the poles
questions.explain: The Mercator projection made it easier to plot a course across oceans, though it distorts the size of areas near the poles.

questions.q: The astrolabe and quadrant helped navigators do what?
options: Calculate longitude exactly by comparing the stars with the position of the moon
Predict the weather for coming days
Estimate latitude by measuring the angle of the sun or stars
Measure the depth of the ocean beneath the ship
questions.explain: These instruments helped sailors determine how far north or south they were; longitude remained difficult until accurate clocks were developed.

questions.q: Which was a major problem for sailors of the 1500s that was not solved until the 1700s?
options: Finding the equator
Determining longitude at sea
Locating the Atlantic
Building ships with sails
questions.explain: Accurate marine clocks eventually allowed navigators to calculate longitude, reducing shipwrecks.

questions.q: The Spanish Inquisition, established in 1478, was meant to do what?
options: Promote religious toleration among Spain's people
Manage Spain's overseas trade and ships
Train Native priests for work in the colonies
Enforce Catholic orthodoxy among Spain's people
questions.explain: Spanish monarchs used it to enforce religious unity, and in 1492 they expelled Jews who would not convert.

questions.q: Early Spanish colonists in Hispaniola relied on the Taino for labor. What happened to the Taino population within decades?
options: It grew rapidly
It moved to Spain
It became the largest group in the Caribbean
It collapsed because of disease, overwork, and violence
questions.explain: Within a few decades the Taino population dropped catastrophically, one reason Spain sought enslaved Africans.

questions.q: Which of these items did Europeans bring to the Americas?
options: Corn and pumpkins
Wheat and grapevines
Turkeys and chocolate
Potatoes and peanuts
questions.explain: Old World crops like wheat and grapes were planted in colonies, while corn, pumpkins, potatoes, and chocolate came from the Americas.

questions.q: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was established by which organization?
options: The Massachusetts Bay Company
The Dutch West India Company
The Virginia Company of London
The Hudson's Bay Company
questions.explain: A joint-stock company with a royal charter financed the venture, hoping for profits from gold, trade, and land.

questions.q: Early settlers at Jamestown faced severe hardship, including the 'Starving Time' of 1609 to 1610. Which factors contributed?
options: A complete lack of any trade with Europe or with its merchants during the early years
Constant attacks by the Spanish navy on the colony
Disease, poor planning, a drought, and conflict with the Powhatan
A ban on farming imposed by the company
questions.explain: Many colonists were gentlemen unused to labor, the site had poor water, and fighting with the Powhatan kept them inside the fort.

questions.q: What cash crop made Virginia's economy profitable after John Rolfe's experiments with a West Indian variety around 1612?
options: Tobacco
Cotton
Rice
Indigo
questions.explain: Tobacco found a strong market in England and set the colony on a path of plantation agriculture requiring large amounts of labor.

questions.q: The Virginia House of Burgesses, which first met in 1619, was significant as what?
options: The first colonial court system in North America
The first representative assembly in the English colonies
A body whose members were appointed by the king alone
A council of Native leaders who advised the governor
questions.explain: Elected representatives from Virginia's settlements met with the governor and council, beginning a tradition of colonial self-government.

questions.q: The Virginia House of Burgesses can be seen as a model for later American legislatures because it did what?
options: Rejected English law altogether in favor of local custom
Elected the governor who led the colony
Gave all residents the right to vote
Gave colonists a role in making laws through elected representatives
questions.explain: Although voting was limited (women, servants, and enslaved people were excluded), the Burgesses set a precedent for representative government.

questions.q: The headright system, introduced in Virginia in 1618, offered what?
options: Free passage and land to all English citizens who asked
Cash payments to colonists for planting tobacco
Land to settlers who paid their own passage or that of others
Voting rights to every immigrant who arrived
questions.explain: Fifty acres per person transported encouraged wealthy planters to bring in indentured servants, which concentrated land among the elite.

questions.q: Most English migrants to the Chesapeake colonies in the 1600s came as what?
options: Indentured servants
Free landowners
Royal officials
Missionaries
questions.explain: Poor English men and women signed contracts to work for several years in exchange for passage and, ideally, 'freedom dues' afterward.

questions.q: Which statement best describes an indentured servant's status?
options: A person enslaved for life and treated as property that could be bought and sold by owners
A person bound to labor for a set number of years in exchange for passage to America
A landowner with the right to vote in elections
A skilled worker paid wages every week
questions.explain: Indentured servitude was temporary, though conditions could be harsh, which distinguished it from the lifelong slavery that later grew.

questions.q: Why were English indentured servants less costly in the early Chesapeake than enslaved Africans, which affected labor choices?
options: Servants never died
Servants were free of any contract
African laborers were unavailable to colonists everywhere
Servants cost less up front and were needed only for a limited time
questions.explain: Early planters found short-term servants cheaper, but longer life spans and a drop in English migration later made lifelong enslaved labor more attractive.

questions.q: In 1619, a ship carrying about twenty enslaved Africans arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia. Why is this event remembered?
options: It is the first documented arrival of Africans in English Virginia
It was the end of slavery in the colony
It established the first reservation for Native peoples
It led directly to the writing of the Mayflower Compact
questions.explain: The arrival, recorded by John Rolfe, marks the start of African presence in English Virginia; legal slavery took shape gradually afterward.

questions.q: Which development in Virginia between 1640 and 1705 most clearly marked the rise of hereditary racial slavery?
options: Laws that guaranteed freedom after seven years of service
Laws that defined Africans and their children as enslaved for life
Laws that banned the sale of enslaved people
Laws granting enslaved people the right to a jury trial
questions.explain: Colonial laws, such as the 1662 rule that a child's status followed the mother's, gradually transformed bondage into an inherited, race-based system.

questions.q: A 1662 Virginia law stated that a child's status as free or enslaved followed the mother's condition. What was one effect of this law?
options: It limited slavery to a single generation, since children of enslaved women were born free
It ended the practice of indentured servitude
It gave enslaved women new legal rights in court
Children born to enslaved women became enslaved regardless of their father's status
questions.explain: The rule made slavery self-perpetuating and removed a legal barrier to exploiting enslaved women.

questions.q: Carolina's early slave laws were modeled on the slave code of which Caribbean colony?
options: Cuba
Hispaniola
Barbados
Martinique
questions.explain: Many early Carolina planters came from Barbados, and the colony copied its harsh 1661 code giving owners near-total power.

questions.q: Bacon's Rebellion (1676) in Virginia was led by Nathaniel Bacon, who opposed Governor William Berkeley mainly because Berkeley did what?
options: Ordered the colony's farmers to stop growing tobacco and plant wheat
Banned any new settlement in the Chesapeake
Refused to support settlers' demands for attacks on Native peoples on the frontier
Imposed a religious test for voting
questions.explain: Frontier farmers resented Berkeley's policy toward Native nations and the elite's control, and Bacon's followers also attacked peaceful tribes.

questions.q: Who made up many of the followers in Bacon's Rebellion?
options: Wealthy planters and merchants of the Tidewater, who joined together to defend their estates and profits
Royal officials and soldiers sent from England
Native American allies from the Powhatan Confederacy
Frontier farmers, former servants, and some enslaved workers who wanted land and opportunity
questions.explain: The coalition of poor whites and Black laborers alarmed the elite, which, many historians argue, encouraged planters to prefer a more controllable enslaved workforce.

questions.q: According to a widely taught interpretation, how did Bacon's Rebellion contribute to the growth of slavery in Virginia?
options: It abolished indentured servitude by law in 1677 and required planters to hire free workers
Planters feared rebellious servants and turned increasingly to enslaved African labor
It led Virginia's elite to free their workers
It ended tobacco farming in the colony for a decade
questions.explain: Many historians argue planters feared a landless, rebellious servant class and shifted toward enslaved labor; falling prices of enslaved people and fewer English migrants also mattered.

questions.q: Maryland, chartered in 1632 to Cecil Calvert, Lord Baltimore, was founded partly to do what?
options: Provide a refuge for English Catholics and profit for the proprietor
Serve as a base for English Puritan reformers seeking to build a model society
Spread Anglican teaching to Native peoples nearby
Establish a profitable Dutch fur trade
questions.explain: Calvert hoped to give Catholics a safe place while making the colony profitable, though Protestants soon outnumbered Catholics there.

questions.q: The Maryland Act of Toleration (1649) is known for guaranteeing what?
options: Freedom of religion for all people including non-Christians
An end to the established church in all colonies
Toleration for Christians who believed in the Trinity
Equal voting rights for women
questions.explain: It was an early colonial step toward religious toleration but limited to Trinitarian Christians, and it prescribed death for denying the Trinity.

questions.q: Why was the Toleration Act of Maryland adopted?
options: The king demanded it as a condition of the charter after complaints from Protestant leaders
Native leaders requested it after the first treaties
Anglican ministers wanted greater freedom of worship
Catholic leaders wanted to protect their rights as a minority among Protestants
questions.explain: With Protestants growing in number, the Catholic proprietor sought legal protection for his co-religionists.

questions.q: Which geographic feature of the Chesapeake region encouraged scattered plantations rather than large towns?
options: Many navigable rivers that let ships load tobacco at planters' own docks
Harsh winters that froze the rivers and stopped trade for months at a time each year
Dense forests that blocked river travel and shipping
A scarcity of fertile land along the coast
questions.explain: Ocean-going ships could reach plantation landings, so large port cities were less necessary there than in the Northeast.

questions.q: Tobacco farming affected the Chesapeake environment by doing what?
options: Increasing soil fertility with each harvest
Exhausting soil and pushing planters to seek new land
Eliminating the mosquitoes that carried disease
Reducing the need for labor on plantations
questions.explain: Tobacco quickly drained nutrients, so planters moved west and wanted more land, intensifying clashes with Native nations.

questions.q: Early Chesapeake society was marked by high death rates and an imbalance of men and women. What was one result?
options: Rapid growth of large cities and towns
Slower natural population growth and delayed family formation
A population dominated by children and young families
A sharp decline in the demand for labor
questions.explain: Disease and a shortage of women meant fewer families and lower birth rates, so growth depended on migration.

questions.q: The Virginia gentry, such as the Washington family, based their wealth and political influence mainly on what?
options: Large tobacco plantations worked by enslaved laborers
Banking and shipping firms located in the larger port towns of the coast
The fur trade with Native nations
Small manufacturing workshops and mills
questions.explain: Planter families controlled land and local offices, and George Washington was born into that Virginia gentry in 1732.

questions.q: What was the role of the county court and the vestry in colonial Virginia?
options: Appointments by the king
Direct elections by all residents
Local governance by elite planters
Control by enslaved communities
questions.explain: Wealthy planters dominated county courts and parish vestries, giving them local authority over justice, roads, and the poor.

questions.q: In colonial Virginia, which church was legally established and supported by taxes?
options: The Congregational Church
The Quaker Meeting
The Catholic Church
The Church of England (Anglican)
questions.explain: Taxpayers supported Anglican parishes even if they belonged to other denominations, which later sparked protest from dissenters.

questions.q: Virginia became a royal colony in 1624. What happened?
options: The king revoked the Virginia Company's charter and took direct control
Parliament made the colony fully independent of the Crown and gave control to the settlers
The Powhatan took over the government of the colony
The Dutch purchased the colony from the company
questions.explain: Company troubles and the 1622 attack led King James I to take control, appointing a governor.

questions.q: In March 1622, Opechancanough led an attack on English settlements in Virginia that killed hundreds of colonists. What was a main cause?
options: A dispute over the price of tobacco
A religious disagreement between Anglicans and Native priests
An English attempt to tax goods traded by Native peoples
Native resentment over English expansion onto their land
questions.explain: The rapid spread of tobacco plantations threatened Powhatan land, and English response included brutal retaliation.

questions.q: How did English settlers generally treat the Powhatan after the attack of 1622?
options: They signed a permanent peace and shared the land
They adopted Powhatan customs and moved into villages
They waged war and sought to drive them from nearby lands
They gave the Powhatan seats in the House of Burgesses
questions.explain: English leaders adopted a policy of warfare and destruction of Native crops, and after another attack in 1644 a 1646 treaty confined the Powhatan to defined areas.

questions.q: John Smith's map of Virginia (1612) is important because it did what?
options: Established the exact border between Virginia and the neighboring colony of Maryland
Provided Europeans with a detailed picture of the Chesapeake region and Native towns
Marked every Spanish fort along the Florida coast
Showed the water route across the continent to the Pacific
questions.explain: Smith's map, printed in England, shaped English understanding and promoted colonization, and the Library of Congress preserves copies.

questions.q: Captain John Smith's rule at Jamestown, 'He that will not work shall not eat,' aimed to do what?
options: Limit trade between the colonists and the Powhatan to a few weeks each year
End the use of indentured servants in the colony
Prevent women from joining the settlement
Force all colonists to contribute labor to the struggling settlement
questions.explain: The harsh policy sought to end idleness among colonists who had hoped to find gold, and it helped keep the colony alive early on.

questions.q: Pocahontas, the daughter of Wahunsenacawh, is remembered for what role in early Virginia?
options: Founding the first Christian church at Jamestown and serving as its first minister for years
Serving as an intermediary between the Powhatan and English before her marriage to John Rolfe
Leading Native warriors in the attack of 1622
Writing the treaty that ended the Powhatan wars
questions.explain: Her kidnapping in 1613 and marriage to John Rolfe in 1614 coincided with a period of relative peace, though the story has often been romanticized.

questions.q: Why did English investors begin to support Virginia more after tobacco proved profitable?
options: It guaranteed that gold would soon be discovered
It lowered the cost of Atlantic travel for settlers
It showed the colony could generate steady income
It ended resistance from nearby Native nations
questions.explain: Profit from tobacco gave the colony an economic base and drew more settlers and investors.

questions.q: The Carolina colony, chartered in 1663, was settled with significant participation of planters from which place?
options: Barbados
Massachusetts
Quebec
Holland
questions.explain: Barbadian planters brought experience with slavery and plantation agriculture, shaping Carolina's society.

questions.q: Which crop, raised with the knowledge and labor of enslaved West Africans, became South Carolina's main export in the 1700s?
options: Rice
Wheat
Flax
Tobacco
questions.explain: Many enslaved people came from rice-growing regions of West Africa, and their skills helped make Lowcountry rice plantations highly profitable.

questions.q: Eliza Lucas Pinckney is remembered for experiments in the 1740s that helped establish which crop in South Carolina?
options: Cotton
Hemp
Indigo
Tea
questions.explain: Indigo, a source of blue dye, complemented rice and was grown in the same region.

questions.q: The Lowcountry of South Carolina developed the 'task system' of labor. What did it involve?
options: Workers were paid weekly wages by the planters and were free to leave and find other work
Gangs of workers labored from sunrise to sunset in long lines
Workers owned the land they farmed
Enslaved workers were assigned daily tasks and, once done, could work for themselves
questions.explain: The system, linked with rice cultivation, gave some enslaved people a bit more control over time, aiding the preservation of Gullah culture.

questions.q: The Gullah language and culture developed in the South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry. What does it illustrate?
options: The widespread adoption of Native American languages, religion, and farming by enslaved communities
The persistence of African cultural traditions in a region with large, isolated enslaved communities
The strong influence of Puritan religious teaching
The rapid breakdown of African culture in America
questions.explain: A black majority and relative isolation helped preserve African-derived language, crafts, and religious practices.

questions.q: The Stono Rebellion in 1739 occurred in which colony?
options: Virginia
New York
South Carolina
Georgia
questions.explain: Enslaved people near the Stono River tried to escape toward Spanish Florida, and the uprising led to harsher laws.

questions.q: One result of the Stono Rebellion was that South Carolina did what?
options: Passed the 1740 Negro Act, tightening controls on enslaved people
Banned slavery altogether within the colony
Gave enslaved people the right to meet and worship freely
Abolished its colonial government
questions.explain: Planters feared more uprisings, so the colony restricted movement, assembly, and literacy.

questions.q: Why did participants in the Stono Rebellion head south?
options: They sought help from French troops in Louisiana
Spain had offered freedom to enslaved people who reached Florida
They planned to sail home to Africa from Charles Town
They hoped to reach the free communities of Virginia
questions.explain: A Spanish proclamation promising liberty to those who escaped English colonies encouraged flight to St. Augustine.

questions.q: Fort Mose, founded in 1738 near St. Augustine, was notable as what?
options: A French fur trading post on the Gulf coast that served Native hunters and traders from Louisiana
A Dutch plantation worked by enslaved laborers
A Native mission for Pueblo converts
A settlement of free Black people who had escaped enslavement in the English colonies
questions.explain: Spanish authorities granted freedom to some fugitives who converted to Catholicism and served in the militia.

questions.q: Georgia was founded in 1732 under James Oglethorpe. Which purpose was among its goals?
options: Create a colony of refuge for Catholic exiles who were fleeing persecution in England
