Compete with Dutch fur traders on the Hudson
Serve as a buffer against Spanish Florida and give England's "worthy poor" a fresh start
Grow sugar for export to England
questions.explain: Trustees sought a military buffer and a philanthropic experiment for England's "worthy poor"; few debtors actually settled there.

questions.q: When Georgia was first founded, its trustees banned what?
options: Slavery and the importation of rum
Tobacco growing
Protestant worship
All trade with Native nations
questions.explain: The ban reflected the trustees' plans for a colony of small farmers, but it was lifted in 1751 as planters pressed for enslaved labor.

questions.q: The Royal African Company, chartered by England in 1672, was established to do what?
options: Run all of Virginia's tobacco exports to London
Manage the shipbuilding industry of New England
Mine silver in Peru for the Spanish crown
Hold a monopoly on the English slave trade with Africa
questions.explain: The monopoly ended in 1698, opening the trade to more English merchants, which increased the volume of enslaved people brought to the colonies.

questions.q: The 'triangular trade' is best described as what?
options: A route for coastal shipping within the Chesapeake Bay
A pattern of Atlantic trade linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas
A network of trade among Native nations in the Southeast
A system of missions in the Spanish borderlands
questions.explain: Ships carried manufactured goods to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, and sugar, rum, and tobacco back to Europe, though real routes were more varied.

questions.q: How did enslaved Africans resist slavery in the colonies?
options: By voting in colonial elections held each spring and choosing local officials
By petitioning the king in person at the royal court
By forming political parties to elect representatives
By running away, slowing work, sabotaging tools, and sometimes rebelling
questions.explain: Resistance took many forms, from everyday acts to organized revolts such as Stono and the New York plots.

questions.q: In 1712 and 1741, enslaved people in New York City were suspected of or carried out plots that led to harsh punishments. These events show what?
options: Slavery existed in northern colonies and provoked fear among white colonists
Slavery was limited entirely to the Southern colonies
Colonists in the North never feared slave uprisings
Enslaved people in New York had the same legal rights as free people
questions.explain: Slavery was widespread in New York, and rumors of conspiracies in 1741 led to executions and banishments.

questions.q: By the early 1700s, enslaved people made up a large share of the population in which pair of colonies?
options: Massachusetts and Connecticut
New Hampshire and Maine
South Carolina and Virginia
Pennsylvania and Rhode Island
questions.explain: South Carolina had a black majority, and Virginia's enslaved population grew rapidly as tobacco planters bought more laborers.

questions.q: Virginia's 1705 slave code did what?
options: Granted freedom to enslaved people who converted to Christianity
Consolidated earlier laws and classified enslaved people as property
Banned the sale of enslaved children away from their mothers
Limited the power of slaveholders over the people they owned
questions.explain: The code defined slavery as a hereditary status and gave owners vast control, building on prior statutes.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how the legal status of Africans in Virginia changed in the 1600s?
options: It moved from slavery toward freedom as the colonies adopted new laws of manumission
It stayed the same
It was decided by the king
It moved from varied statuses toward a fixed condition of lifelong slavery
questions.explain: Some Africans in early Virginia gained freedom, but laws hardened status over time, closing off that path.

questions.q: Why did the English colonies' demand for enslaved Africans rise sharply after 1680?
options: Native peoples agreed to work on the plantations in exchange for English goods and tools
Indenture became illegal
English migration declined as wages rose at home, and plantation crops needed more labor
The Royal Navy required it
questions.explain: With fewer English servants available and profitable staples, planters bought more enslaved Africans from an expanding Atlantic trade.

questions.q: Southern planters in the 1700s often borrowed from British merchants to buy land and enslaved workers. What was one result?
options: The colonies became financially independent of British merchants and banks
Many planters fell into debt to their English creditors
English merchants lost money
Planters stopped growing tobacco
questions.explain: Debt tied the colonial economy to the British market and was a source of resentment.

questions.q: Which statement describes the 'Indian slave trade' in the Southeast in the late 1600s and early 1700s?
options: Carolina traders captured and sold Native captives, sometimes to other colonies and the Caribbean
It was banned by every English colony in the 1600s after repeated complaints from Native nations
It ended in 1607
It was run by Spain only
questions.explain: Native enslavement was a major trade out of Charles Town, fueling wars among Native nations and disrupting communities.

questions.q: The Yamasee War (1715-1717) in South Carolina began largely because Yamasee and other Native groups did what?
options: Wanted to join the Spanish in Florida and gave up their English trade for Spanish goods
Opposed Christianity
Had been refused trading goods
Resented debts and abuses by English traders and the enslavement of their people
questions.explain: Native debtors and victims of slave raiding struck at English settlements, nearly destroying the colony before it recovered.

questions.q: The Tuscarora War (1711-1713) in North Carolina ended with what major consequence?
options: Many Tuscarora left and later joined the Haudenosaunee Confederacy
The Tuscarora conquered Carolina and forced the colonists to leave the region entirely
A treaty ended English settlement
They were allowed to keep all land
questions.explain: Defeated by colonists and their Native allies, many Tuscarora migrated north and became the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee around 1722.

questions.q: Which colony's founding in 1634 was led by Leonard Calvert on behalf of his brother Cecil?
options: Virginia
Carolina
Maryland
Delaware
questions.explain: Colonists arrived on the Ark and the Dove and established St. Mary's City, where Catholics and Protestants lived together.

questions.q: Which was a typical way wealthy Virginians displayed status in the 1700s?
options: Public lectures on science and philosophy in their own libraries
Large houses, enslaved servants, and holding public office
Founding textile mills
Living in cities
questions.explain: Planter elites used landholding, hospitality, and offices to show rank, and deference shaped political life.

questions.q: Which statement best describes life for most enslaved people on Chesapeake tobacco plantations?
options: They received weekly wages and rented small farms of their own near the plantation
They worked mainly as sailors
They lived in cities
They worked long hours in gangs under supervision and lived in small quarters
questions.explain: Tobacco required intensive labor nearly year-round, and enslaved families lived with the constant threat of sale and separation.

questions.q: Why did some colonial slaveholders resist baptizing enslaved people in the 1600s?
options: Churches refused to baptize them and the colonial government agreed with that policy
Baptism was illegal
They feared Christian baptism might give grounds for claiming freedom
They wanted them to remain Catholic
questions.explain: Virginia clarified in 1667 that baptism did not alter a person's status, which removed that fear.

questions.q: A planter in 1720s Virginia pays more for enslaved workers than for servants. Which reasoning best explains this choice?
options: Servants refused to work in tobacco fields and left their contracts in large numbers
Enslaved labor was permanent and could be passed on to offspring
Enslaved workers were more likely to marry
Servants cost more to feed
questions.explain: Planters saw lifetime service as more valuable than a fixed term, despite the higher initial price.

questions.q: In what way did Virginia's government resemble England's?
options: It had a governor, an appointed council, and an elected assembly
It had a king who lived in Virginia and ruled through a council of local ministers
It was run by town meetings
It had no courts
questions.explain: The governor and council parallel the Crown and House of Lords, and the Burgesses the House of Commons, a structure repeated in many colonies.

questions.q: In most royal colonies, the governor's council, which advised him and served as the upper house of the legislature, was typically what?
options: Elected by all adult men who owned property in the colony
Chosen by lot
Composed only of ministers
Appointed rather than elected by colonists
questions.explain: Councilors were generally prominent men named by the Crown or governor, making the council a conservative body in many colonies.

questions.q: By 1700, which labor system had replaced indentured servitude as the main source of labor in the southern colonies?
options: Chattel slavery
Wage labor
Apprenticeship
Convict labor
questions.explain: As planters turned toward enslaved Africans, the number of indentured servants declined across the South.

questions.q: How did the mild climate and long growing season of the southern colonies shape their economies?
options: They favored large-scale manufacturing and the building of factories in each colony
They supported staple crops such as tobacco, rice, and indigo for export
They prevented farming
They supported only subsistence farming
questions.explain: Warm weather and fertile soils made large-scale cultivation of cash crops possible, which encouraged plantation agriculture.

questions.q: A Virginia law of 1691 forbade interracial marriage and punished those who freed enslaved people unless they were transported out of the colony. What does it reveal?
options: A decline in racial thinking among colonial lawmakers over time
Support for abolishing slavery
Growing efforts to enforce a racial hierarchy
The influence of Quaker ideals
questions.explain: Colonial laws increasingly defined race and attempted to limit free Black people's rights and contact with white colonists.

questions.q: Which type of source would best help a historian understand the daily lives of enslaved people in the 1700s?
options: Narratives and records left by enslaved people themselves, along with archaeological evidence
Only royal decrees and official letters sent by colonial governors to the king and his ministers in London
Only planters' account books
Only legislative debates
questions.explain: Because many enslaved people could not publish their accounts, historians combine sources like narratives, court records, and archaeology.

questions.q: Why did English colonial officials in Barbados and Jamaica encourage sugar production?
options: Sugar was needed for Native trade and for paying tribute to the Spanish crown
Parliament banned tobacco
Sugar was cheap to grow
Sugar exports were highly profitable for the empire
questions.explain: Sugar colonies generated great wealth, which made them among the most valuable parts of England's empire in the 1600s and 1700s.

questions.q: Which of these colonies belonged to the 'Southern colonies' group?
options: New Hampshire
South Carolina
Pennsylvania
Massachusetts
questions.explain: The Southern colonies included Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia.

questions.q: The Pilgrims who founded Plymouth Colony in 1620 were primarily seeking what?
options: Land for large sugar plantations like those on the islands of the Caribbean
A chance to convert the Spanish colonies to Protestantism
The freedom to worship apart from the Church of England
A fur trading monopoly
questions.explain: Separatists believed the Church of England was beyond reform, so they left England for Holland and then America.

questions.q: The Mayflower Compact of 1620 is often cited as an early example of what?
options: A royal charter issued by the king that gave settlers permission to govern themselves
Self-government based on the consent of the governed
A treaty with the Wampanoag
A law establishing an official church
questions.explain: Male colonists aboard the Mayflower agreed to form a body politic and obey its laws, a precedent for self-rule by agreement.

questions.q: Why did the Pilgrims and others aboard the Mayflower sign the Mayflower Compact?
options: The king had ordered them to sign it before they would be allowed to come ashore anywhere in America
They wanted to become independent from England
They had landed outside the area covered by their charter and needed a way to keep order
They were forced by Native leaders
questions.explain: Because they landed in New England instead of Virginia, some passengers questioned the legal authority of the group, so they agreed to a compact.

questions.q: Which Native American man, who spoke English, helped the Pilgrims survive their first years at Plymouth?
options: Metacom
Powhatan
Opechancanough
Squanto (Tisquantum)
questions.explain: A Patuxet who had been in Europe, Squanto taught the colonists to plant corn and served as an interpreter between the Wampanoag and the English.

questions.q: Massasoit, leader of the Wampanoag, agreed to a treaty with Plymouth Colony in 1621 mainly because he wanted what?
options: An ally against rival Native nations such as the Narragansett
Land in England that had been promised to the colonists by the king
Protection from Spanish raids
Conversion to Christianity
questions.explain: Disease had weakened the Wampanoag, so an alliance with the English offered security, and the peace lasted for decades.

questions.q: The Puritans who founded Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1630 differed from the Pilgrims in that the Puritans mainly wanted to do what?
options: Break away completely from the church and build a new religion apart from it
Reform the Church of England from within by building a model society
Establish a colony free of any religion
Convert the Spanish
questions.explain: Puritans considered the church tainted by Catholic practices but hoped their colony would be an example to England.

questions.q: John Winthrop's 1630 sermon described the Massachusetts Bay Colony as 'a city upon a hill.' What did he mean?
options: The colony would be built on a mountain top so it could be defended against attack
The colony was in danger of attack
The colony would be independent
The colony would serve as a model that others would watch
questions.explain: Winthrop told colonists that their community was watched by the world, so success depended on obeying God's covenant.

questions.q: Between about 1630 and 1640, thousands of English Puritans moved to New England. What is this migration called?
options: The Great Migration
The Exodus
The Columbian Exchange
The Second Awakening
questions.explain: Many families, often traveling together, left England during religious and economic troubles under Charles I.

questions.q: Compared with the Chesapeake, early New England had more stable population growth because of what?
options: Fewer women and many unmarried men who arrived without families
Greater use of enslaved labor
Families migrated together and the climate was healthier
Higher reliance on tobacco
questions.explain: New England colonists came in family groups and lived longer in the cooler climate, leading to steady growth.

questions.q: In Puritan Massachusetts, who could vote in colonial elections in the early years?
options: All adult men
All property owners
Male church members
All free people
questions.explain: The colony tied political participation to church membership, reflecting its goal of a godly commonwealth.

questions.q: The New England town meeting was important because it allowed what?
options: The king to appoint local officials and judges for each town in the colony
Eligible male residents to debate and vote on local matters
Women to hold office
Ministers to veto laws
questions.explain: Town meetings gave many men direct participation in local government, shaping traditions of self-rule.

questions.q: Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts in 1635 for what reason?
options: He challenged the colony's authority over religion and its claim to Native land
He committed a serious crime against a neighbor and was convicted by a jury of local men
He led a rebellion
He criticized the king's taxes
questions.explain: Williams argued that civil government should not enforce religious belief and that the king could not grant land without purchase from Native people.

questions.q: Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636, which grew into which colony known for religious toleration?
options: Connecticut
New Hampshire
Maine
Rhode Island
questions.explain: Rhode Island welcomed dissenters such as Quakers and Jews and separated church from state, in contrast to neighboring Puritan colonies.

questions.q: Anne Hutchinson, tried in 1637, was considered a threat to Massachusetts leaders because she did what?
options: Refused to pay taxes to the colony, and urged her followers in Boston to refuse them too, until banished
Led a rebellion against the governor
Opposed colonization
Taught that individuals could receive God's grace directly and questioned ministers' authority
questions.explain: Her meetings in Boston drew followers, and officials charged her with heresy and sedition and banished her.

questions.q: Which term was used by Puritan authorities against Anne Hutchinson's belief that salvation came through grace alone without need for outward conformity?
options: Deism
Pietism
Antinomianism
Arminianism
questions.explain: Authorities feared that her ideas undermined moral law and church order, as she claimed to have direct revelations.

questions.q: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) are often described as what?
options: A treaty between the colonists and the Pequot nation that ended the war of 1637
One of the first written constitutions in the colonies
A royal charter
A religious covenant
questions.explain: Settlers around Hartford created a government based on a written framework, which gave the colony a representative structure.

questions.q: Thomas Hooker led settlers from Massachusetts to Connecticut partly because he wanted what?
options: A government with broader voting rights and less control by church leaders
Freedom from English law and from any need to obey the king or his appointed governors
Better access to fur
A Catholic refuge
questions.explain: His Connecticut settlement did not limit voting to church members, as Massachusetts Bay did, giving a wider group of men a voice in government.

questions.q: The Pequot War of 1636 to 1637 ended with what result?
options: A lasting treaty between equals that guaranteed Pequot land and trade rights for many decades
The destruction of the Pequot as a power in southern New England after the Mystic massacre
Pequot control of Connecticut
The founding of Providence
questions.explain: English colonists and Native allies attacked a fortified Pequot village in 1637, and the survivors were killed, enslaved, or dispersed.

questions.q: King Philip's War (1675-1676) was fought between New England colonists and Native peoples led by Metacom. What was a major cause?
options: Competition over the fur trade with French merchants along the northern border
A disagreement over a church
Growing English settlement and pressure on Native land and independence
Spanish attacks
questions.explain: As colonial towns spread, Native leaders resisted attempts to control their land and sovereignty, and war spread across New England.

questions.q: King Philip's War is notable in colonial history because it did what?
options: Brought a lasting peace between colonists and Native peoples that lasted for a century
Was won by Native peoples
Led to Native representation in colonial assemblies
Caused heavy losses for both sides and broke Native power in southern New England
questions.explain: In proportion to population it was among the deadliest wars in American history, and it ended large-scale Native resistance in the region.

questions.q: Metacom was the son of which Wampanoag leader who had welcomed the Pilgrims?
options: Massasoit
Squanto
Uncas
Canonicus
questions.explain: Metacom, called King Philip by the English, became sachem in 1662, amid growing tensions over land.

questions.q: John Eliot's 'praying towns' in Massachusetts sought to do what?
options: Prepare Native soldiers for war against the French and their allies on the frontier
Convert Native people to Christianity and bring them into English-style communities
Provide Native homes for trade
Protect Native languages by law
questions.explain: Praying towns forced many cultural changes, and during King Philip's War many residents suffered suspicion and mistreatment.

questions.q: The Half-Way Covenant of 1662 was adopted by Puritan churches to do what?
options: Grant women the right to vote in church affairs and hold office in their congregations, as men did
End the practice of baptism
Allow children of baptized but unconverted members to be baptized, easing declining church membership
Allow Catholics to join
questions.explain: As the second generation hesitated to claim conversion experiences, churches extended partial membership to keep more families within the community.

questions.q: The Half-Way Covenant reveals which concern among Puritan leaders in the mid-1600s?
options: Declining religious commitment among the second and third generations
A crisis over taxes imposed by Parliament and the colonial governor on the colony's trade
A threat of invasion
A shortage of ministers from England
questions.explain: Many descendants had not experienced the dramatic conversion required for full membership, which worried leaders about the colony's religious mission.

questions.q: The Salem witch trials of 1692 are an example of what?
options: A war with Native peoples along the frontier that caused many deaths and burned several towns
A conflict between the king and Parliament
A community crisis in which fear and suspicion led to executions based on accusations
A rebellion against taxes
questions.explain: Nineteen people were hanged and others died in custody after accusations spread in Salem Village and nearby towns.

questions.q: Which kind of evidence, accepted at first at Salem, was later widely criticized?
options: Spectral evidence, the claim that a spirit shape of the accused had harmed the accusers
Written confessions only, signed by suspects in front of two ministers and a magistrate
Eyewitness testimony of a crime
Physical evidence
questions.explain: Judges accepted testimony about visions, but in fall 1692 Governor Phips dissolved the special court, and later trials gave such evidence little weight.

questions.q: One lasting legal lesson often drawn from the Salem trials is the importance of what?
options: Strong church authority over every colonial court
Banning all trials
Sworn loyalty to the king
Due process and reliable evidence in court
questions.explain: The episode is often cited in discussions of fair trials, the rights of the accused, and the dangers of mass hysteria.

questions.q: Which factors have historians cited as contributing to the Salem witchcraft crisis?
options: A shortage of ministers in the village and bitter disputes with neighboring colonies
Fear of Native attacks, local rivalries, and strict religious beliefs
An overabundance of tobacco
A war with Spain
questions.explain: Salem Village was divided by disputes, and nearby frontier violence and religious anxieties created fertile ground for accusations.

questions.q: In 1684, England revoked the Massachusetts Bay charter. What was one reason?
options: Massachusetts had failed to pay for the Puritan church and its ministers' salaries
The Crown wanted tighter control over colonial trade and government
Massachusetts invaded New York
Puritans refused to build forts
questions.explain: English officials were frustrated by the colony's resistance to the Navigation Acts and religious intolerance.

questions.q: The Dominion of New England (1686) was an attempt by the Crown to do what?
options: Combine several northern colonies under a royal governor
Give New England independence from England and make it a republic
Create a Native territory
Establish a Puritan state
questions.explain: King James II merged colonies from New England to New Jersey under Sir Edmund Andros to strengthen royal control and enforce trade laws.

questions.q: Sir Edmund Andros, governor of the Dominion of New England, angered colonists because he did what?
options: Granted religious freedom to all settlers and welcomed Native leaders as advisers
Allied with Native nations
Reduced taxes
Ended the colonial assemblies and levied taxes without their consent
questions.explain: He disbanded representative bodies and challenged land titles, which led colonists to see him as a threat to English liberties.

questions.q: How did colonists in New England respond to the Dominion of New England when news of the Glorious Revolution reached Boston in 1689?
options: They welcomed his rule and offered to pay higher taxes
They allied with France
They overthrew and arrested Andros
They declared independence
questions.explain: Colonists in Boston revolted, seeing a chance to restore their charter rights after James II fled England.

questions.q: What was the Glorious Revolution (1688-1689)?
options: The founding of the first permanent English colony on the Chesapeake Bay in 1607
The defeat of Spain's Armada
The overthrow of King James II and the accession of William and Mary
A revolt by American colonists
questions.explain: Parliament invited William of Orange and Mary to rule, confirming parliamentary power and, in 1689, the English Bill of Rights.

questions.q: After 1691, Massachusetts received a new charter that changed its government in what way?
options: The colony became an independent republic, and Massachusetts voters elected the governor and council
Church membership was required for office
Voters selected the governor
The Crown appointed the governor, and voting depended on property rather than church membership
questions.explain: The new charter ended the Puritan monopoly on political power and made Massachusetts a royal colony.

questions.q: The Massachusetts law of 1647, sometimes called the 'Old Deluder Satan Act,' required what?
options: Free college education for any boy of the colony who could read and write Latin well
Towns of a certain size to provide schools so children could read Scripture
Public libraries
A school for Native children
questions.explain: Puritans valued literacy so that people could read the Bible, making New England's literacy rates among the highest in the colonies.

questions.q: Harvard College, founded in 1636, was established primarily to do what?
options: Train ministers and educated leaders for the colony
Teach sailors and ship captains to chart the coast and trade abroad
Prepare soldiers
Educate Native leaders only
questions.explain: Puritan leaders wanted an educated clergy so churches would not be left to ignorance.

questions.q: The Bay Psalm Book (1640), the first book printed in the British colonies of North America, was produced in which place?
options: Philadelphia
Jamestown
Charleston
Cambridge, Massachusetts
questions.explain: A press at Harvard's town printed this metrical translation of the Psalms for use in Puritan worship.

questions.q: The New England Primer, a popular colonial textbook, taught children what?
options: Reading through songs about sailors and stories of English kings
Mathematics only
Reading through religious verses and moral lessons
Native languages
questions.explain: It paired alphabet verses with Bible lessons, which illustrates the connection between literacy and religion.

questions.q: Anne Bradstreet, a Massachusetts poet, is notable because she was what?
options: The first published poet in the English colonies
A Puritan minister who wrote sermons for the Boston church
A Native American translator
A colonial governor
questions.explain: Her volume The Tenth Muse appeared in 1650 in London, showing that women could participate in colonial literary culture.

questions.q: Mary Rowlandson's captivity narrative, published in 1682, described what?
options: Her work as a midwife and healer in the frontier towns of colonial Massachusetts
Her experience as a captive of Native warriors during King Philip's War
Her travels to Virginia
Her trial for witchcraft
questions.explain: Her account became a bestseller, mixing religious reflection with a colonial perspective of events during the war.

questions.q: The Massachusetts 'pine tree shilling,' minted from 1652, indicates what about the colony?
options: It was the first paper currency ever issued by any English colony in North America
It followed royal orders
It asserted economic independence by coining its own money without royal approval
It was used for Native trade
questions.explain: Minting coins defied English authority, which later cracked down on the practice.

questions.q: Which economic activity was a mainstay of New England's economy?
options: Large plantations growing tobacco
Fishing, shipbuilding, and trade
Rice farming
Fur trapping only
questions.explain: Rocky soil limited large-scale farming, so New England relied on cod fishing, timber, and shipping.

questions.q: Which geographic factor most limited commercial agriculture in New England?
options: Short growing seasons and rocky soil
Dry deserts and sandy soils in the interior
Hurricanes
Lack of forests
questions.explain: Farms were mostly small and for family use, and many colonists turned to trade, fishing, and crafts instead.

questions.q: Which feature was typical of New England society?
options: Isolated plantations spread far apart along the rivers, with few villages
Great landed estates
Itinerant societies
Tight-knit towns centered on a meetinghouse and common lands
questions.explain: Town grants and church life shaped community, with settlers living near one another in villages.

questions.q: Under English common law as applied in the colonies, a married woman's legal status was that of what?
options: She generally lost control of her property to her husband (coverture)
She could own property freely and manage it without her husband's consent
She could vote
She could serve on juries
questions.explain: Coverture limited women's legal and economic independence, though widows could often manage estates.

questions.q: Which statement best describes women's roles in the colonial economy?
options: They were excluded from all economic activity, including trade and farm management
They held most political offices
They managed households and produced goods, and some ran shops or farms as widows
They ran large shipping firms
questions.explain: Women's labor in spinning, farming, and trade was essential, though laws limited their formal rights.

questions.q: In 1660, Mary Dyer, a Quaker, was executed in Boston. What does it show?
options: The colony supported toleration and welcomed religious dissenters from other places
A rebellion against the king
A war with Rhode Island
Puritan authorities punished those who defied their religious order
questions.explain: Quakers rejected Puritan church authority and were banned, and Mary Dyer returned after banishment and was hanged.

questions.q: Which belief made Quakers a target in New England?
options: They refused to speak English and kept themselves apart from other colonists entirely
They believed in an 'inner light' and rejected ministers and formal rituals
They sought Catholic rule
They supported slavery
questions.explain: The Quakers' emphasis on equality and individual conscience threatened Puritan authority.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Puritan concept of a 'covenant'?
options: A royal charter that granted the settlers the right to govern their colony in the king's name
A trade contract
A legal document with Native leaders
An agreement between God and the community, and among members, to live according to Scripture
questions.explain: Puritans believed that their colony had a covenant with God, and misbehavior might bring divine punishment.

questions.q: A jeremiad, a type of sermon common in Puritan New England, usually did what?
options: Praised the king and the governor for protecting the colony during times of war and trouble
Warned that the community was straying from its religious mission and faced God's judgment
Recounted the voyage
Taught navigation
questions.explain: Ministers used jeremiads to call people to renewal during hardships such as wars and epidemics.

questions.q: Cotton Mather, a Boston minister, is associated with which of the following?
options: Writing about witchcraft and also promoting smallpox inoculation
Founding Harvard College and writing the first New England laws on schooling
Leading King Philip's War
Writing the Mayflower Compact
questions.explain: Mather defended aspects of the Salem trials' era beliefs yet supported inoculation during the 1721 epidemic, showing the blend of religion and science.

questions.q: Which New England colony received a 1662 charter that joined the Hartford and New Haven settlements?
options: Rhode Island
Maine
Connecticut
New Hampshire
questions.explain: Charles II granted a charter to Connecticut that secured self-government, including election of its governor.

questions.q: Colonial charters granted to Connecticut and Rhode Island in the 1660s were notable because they allowed what?
options: Appointment of governors and legislators by the king and his Privy Council
Election of governors and legislatures by the colonists themselves
A permanent military
Establishing an official church
questions.explain: These corporate charters gave unusual self-rule that colonists would later defend.

questions.q: Why did some New England colonists settle in places like New Hampshire and Maine?
options: To escape Spanish rule along the southern coast
To follow the king's orders
To find more land and economic opportunity
To join Native communities
questions.explain: Fishing, trade, and timber attracted settlers beyond the original Puritan towns.

questions.q: The New England economy was tied to the West Indies because it did what?
options: Exported fish, lumber, and livestock and imported sugar and molasses
Imported tobacco and exported grain and livestock to the Chesapeake colonies and the Caribbean
Exported gold
Imported cotton
questions.explain: Trade with Caribbean sugar islands, which needed food and lumber, was a major source of New England wealth.

questions.q: What was a significant way that New England merchants profited from the slave economy?
options: By owning African gold mines and trading in the gold at ports of the Caribbean
By holding the royal monopoly
By taxing the trade
By supplying provisions to sugar colonies and distilling rum from molasses
questions.explain: Even though New England had fewer plantations, its merchants and shipbuilders were closely linked to slavery's profits.

questions.q: Why did Puritan leaders limit the number of people who could vote in early Massachusetts?
options: They believed government should be led by those who were part of the church and in covenant
They wanted a hereditary aristocracy led by wealthy families who held large estates and royal appointments
The king required it
They feared Native voters
questions.explain: Their vision of a godly society tied political rights to religious standing.

questions.q: The Mayflower brought both Separatists and non-Separatists. The colonists the Pilgrims called 'Strangers' were what?
options: Native Americans who had joined the voyage as guides and interpreters
Spanish sailors
Indentured Dutch farmers
Passengers who were not part of their religious congregation
questions.explain: About half of the passengers were Strangers who sought economic opportunity rather than religious separation.

questions.q: Where did the Pilgrims live for about a decade before sailing to America?
options: France
Ireland
The Netherlands
Spain
questions.explain: They fled to Leiden in Holland to avoid persecution, but worried that their children were losing English ways.

questions.q: How did the Pilgrims at Plymouth finance their voyage?
options: Through royal gifts from King James, who paid for the voyage and supplies from the royal treasury
Through a loan from English merchant investors, to be repaid with fish, fur, and timber
Through taxes
Through the Spanish crown
questions.explain: The investors expected a return, and the debt put pressure on the colony until it was paid off.

questions.q: William Bradford, who wrote Of Plymouth Plantation, is notable as what?
options: Founder of Rhode Island and author of the colony's first charter, who was banished from Boston
Leader of the Pequot War
Governor of Plymouth for much of its early history and author of its chronicle
Governor of Virginia
questions.explain: Bradford's history is a major source for early Plymouth life and for Pilgrim religious views.

questions.q: Puritan communities limited the spread of which of the following to protect religious conformity?
options: Dissenting views, through laws and banishment
Ocean-going trade
Farming
Fishing
questions.explain: Leaders regarded dissent as a danger to the covenant community and expelled or punished dissenters.

questions.q: Puritans often described New England as a 'wilderness' that they were taming. Which statement identifies what this view overlooked?
options: No people lived there because disease had completely emptied the whole region long before 1600
The area was ruled by Spain
The land was already farmed by Europeans
Native peoples had already shaped the land and lived there for generations
questions.explain: Colonial writers framed settlement as the creation of order, yet Native farming, villages, and land management had long existed.

questions.q: New Netherland, the Dutch colony in North America, was centered on which port?
options: Quebec
New Amsterdam
Boston
St. Augustine
questions.explain: New Amsterdam, on Manhattan Island, became the commercial heart of the colony and later was renamed New York.

questions.q: New Netherland attracted a more diverse population than most colonies mainly because of its focus on what?
options: A religious test requiring all settlers to belong to the Dutch Reformed Church
Gold mining
Commerce and trade, which welcomed people of many backgrounds
A law requiring English settlement
questions.explain: Dutch trading interests led to a mix of Europeans, Africans, and others, and the colony tolerated different faiths more than many neighbors.

questions.q: The Dutch patroon system offered large estates along the Hudson River to those who did what?
options: Fought in a war against the Spanish and received a royal charter in return
Brought over a specified number of settlers to work the land
Converted Native people
Paid a fee to the king
questions.explain: Patroons held manorial powers, but the system attracted few settlers compared with other colonies.

questions.q: In 1664, English forces seized New Netherland and renamed it for whom?
options: The Duke of Marlborough, who led English armies in Europe
Sir Walter Raleigh
William Penn
The Duke of York, brother of King Charles II
questions.explain: Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant surrendered without a fight, and the colony became New York under proprietor James, Duke of York.

questions.q: Why did England want to take control of New Netherland in 1664?
options: It separated English colonies in New England from those in the Chesapeake and threatened English trade
The Dutch had refused for decades to pay a long-standing debt owed to the English crown and its merchants
It had rich silver mines
The Dutch banned English ships entirely
questions.explain: Controlling the Hudson River and a major port would complete English control of the Atlantic coast and enforce the Navigation Acts.

questions.q: When England took over New York, the Dutch residents were generally allowed to do what?
options: Leave the colony immediately and give up their houses and businesses
Keep their property and continue many religious and cultural practices
Hold all public offices
Be exempt from taxes
questions.explain: The English terms of surrender were generous, so Dutch culture remained influential in the Hudson Valley for generations.

questions.q: The 1626 'purchase' of Manhattan by Peter Minuit is a story that historians treat cautiously because it shows what?
options: Europeans and Native peoples likely understood the exchange differently
It never happened
It was a purely symbolic ceremony that had no connection to land at all
It was recorded as a gift
questions.explain: The Lenape may have understood the exchange as an agreement to share use of the land rather than a permanent sale.

questions.q: William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a refuge for which religious group?
options: Puritans
Catholics
Baptists
Quakers
questions.explain: Penn, himself a Quaker, saw the colony as a 'Holy Experiment' in religious freedom and peaceful relations.

questions.q: Which of these was a core belief of Quakers (the Society of Friends)?
options: Ordained priests must lead worship and interpret Scripture for the congregation
Predestination
Every person has an 'inner light,' and all are spiritually equal
Obedience to the king over conscience
questions.explain: Quaker equality shaped their views on women's preaching, pacifism, and treatment of Native people, though some Quakers owned slaves.

questions.q: William Penn's relations with the Lenape (Delaware) were noted for what?
options: Efforts to buy land through negotiation and treat Native people fairly
Constant warfare and attempts to drive the Lenape out of the colony altogether
Forcible removal
Ignoring Native claims
questions.explain: Penn's approach produced a generation of relative peace, though after his death his sons used deceptive tactics such as the Walking Purchase of 1737.

questions.q: Pennsylvania's 1701 Charter of Privileges guaranteed what?
options: A permanent established Quaker church
The right of Parliament to tax the colony and appoint its governor and judges
Freedom of conscience and a unicameral elected assembly
Rule by the Penn family only
questions.explain: The charter protected religious liberty for those who believed in God and gave the assembly strong powers, and it remained the colony's frame of government until 1776.

questions.q: The middle colonies were sometimes called the 'breadbasket' colonies because they exported what?
options: Tobacco grown on large estates and shipped to London merchants each year
Rice
Indigo
Wheat and other grains and flour
questions.explain: Fertile soil and a moderate climate made the Hudson and Delaware valleys leading producers of grain for domestic and overseas markets.

questions.q: Compared with New England and the Chesapeake, the middle colonies were distinctive in that their populations were what?
options: Almost entirely English, with very few settlers from other countries
The most ethnically and religiously diverse
Entirely Puritan
Mostly Spanish
questions.explain: Dutch, English, Germans, Scots-Irish, Swedes, Africans, and others lived there, with many religious groups coexisting.

questions.q: Which immigrant group, many of them from Germany, settled in large numbers in Pennsylvania in the 1700s?
options: Portuguese sailors and merchants seeking work in the busy port of Philadelphia
Italians
Russians
Germans seeking land and religious freedom
questions.explain: Lutherans, Mennonites, Moravians, and others migrated to Pennsylvania, forming communities that kept their language and customs.

questions.q: Scots-Irish immigrants in the 1700s often settled where in the colonies?
options: In the coastal towns of New England, close to the harbors of Boston and Salem
In Boston
In the western backcountry from Pennsylvania down the Appalachian valleys
In Charles Town
questions.explain: Arriving from Ulster, they took up frontier land, which brought them into conflict with Native peoples and sometimes with coastal elites.

questions.q: The 1735 trial of John Peter Zenger is remembered as an important step toward what?
options: Trial by combat
Freedom of the press
The abolition of slavery
Separation of church and state
questions.explain: Zenger, a New York printer, was acquitted of seditious libel after his newspaper criticized the royal governor.

questions.q: Zenger's lawyer, Andrew Hamilton, argued that a printer should not be punished for publishing statements that were what?
options: True
Popular
Approved by the governor
Brief
questions.explain: Though the law at the time held that criticism of officials was libel even if true, the jury sided with Hamilton's argument.

questions.q: Zenger was prosecuted for criticizing which official?
options: King George II, who had personally ordered the printer's arrest in London
Royal governor William Cosby
Governor Berkeley
Edmund Andros
questions.explain: Zenger's New-York Weekly Journal attacked Cosby's abuses of power, and officials charged Zenger with seditious libel.

questions.q: Why is the Zenger verdict often said to show the power of colonial juries?
options: The judge declared him innocent and dismissed the charge before the jury met
Parliament overruled the court
The governor pardoned him
The jury acquitted him despite the judge's instructions about the law of libel
questions.explain: Jurors reflected community opinion rather than royal interests, which pointed toward a public check on government.

questions.q: Which later constitutional provision is most closely connected to the principle of press freedom promoted in the Zenger case?
options: The First Amendment
The Third Amendment
The Fifth Amendment
The Tenth Amendment
questions.explain: The Zenger case is often cited as an early example of the idea later protected in the Bill of Rights.

questions.q: The Navigation Acts, beginning in 1651, required that colonial trade be carried mainly in what?
options: English or colonial ships
Dutch ships, because the Dutch had the largest merchant fleet in the world
Spanish ships
Native canoes
questions.explain: The laws aimed to weaken Dutch commercial rivals and funnel colonial trade through England.

questions.q: Under the Navigation Act of 1660, 'enumerated goods' such as sugar and tobacco had to be shipped where?
options: To any European port where the best price could be obtained for the cargo
To Spain
To Africa
To England or another English colony only
questions.explain: This rule ensured England would profit from re-exporting valuable colonial products.

questions.q: The Staple Act of 1663 required what?
options: That colonists pay no taxes of any kind on goods bought from European merchants
That most European goods destined for the colonies be shipped through England
That tobacco be grown only in Virginia
That Native peoples trade only with colonists
questions.explain: This law made England the middleman, allowing English merchants and officials to collect duties on goods heading to America.

questions.q: The 1696 Navigation Act created vice-admiralty courts in the colonies, which were significant because they did what?
options: Provided a jury trial for every accused smuggler, as in English common law courts
Governed Native relations
Tried smuggling cases without juries, strengthening enforcement
Selected governors
questions.explain: Colonists resented courts run by royal judges rather than local juries, a complaint that grew louder later in the 1700s.

questions.q: The Board of Trade, created in 1696, was established to do what?
options: Oversee colonial commerce and advise on policy for the colonies
Elect colonial governors and judges on behalf of the voters in each colony
Collect Native tribute
Run colonial churches
questions.explain: The board centralized English supervision of colonial trade and government, though its authority was often weakly enforced.

questions.q: The term 'salutary neglect' describes what British practice in the early 1700s?
options: Strict and constant enforcement of every trade law on colonial merchants
Loosely enforcing trade regulations on the colonies
Abandoning the colonies
Sending large armies to colonies
questions.explain: Officials cared more about colonial trade profits than strict control, so colonists were left to manage much of their own affairs.

questions.q: What was one effect of salutary neglect on colonial political life?
options: Colonists lost most of their traditional rights as royal officials took control
Parliament dissolved the assemblies
Colonists became more loyal to the king
Colonial assemblies gained experience and power in governing themselves
questions.explain: With distant officials rarely interfering, colonial legislatures claimed rights like controlling taxes and the governor's salary.

questions.q: Colonial assemblies gained leverage over royal governors mainly by controlling what?
options: The colony's militia and its officers, whom the assembly appointed each year
Native diplomacy
Taxes and the governor's salary
The press
questions.explain: Because governors depended on assemblies for their pay, legislators could press for their own priorities.

questions.q: Who generally could vote in colonial elections in the 1700s?
options: All adult men, regardless of whether they owned land or any other property
White men who owned a certain amount of property
All adults
Only landowners over 60
questions.explain: Property requirements varied by colony, but because land was easier to obtain in America, a larger share of men could vote than in England.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a proprietary colony from a royal colony?
options: Proprietary colonies had no government of their own; royal colonies were run by elected assemblies alone
A royal colony had no governor
A proprietary colony was settled by Dutch
Proprietary colonies were granted to owners with governing rights; royal colonies had Crown-appointed governors
questions.explain: Maryland and Pennsylvania were proprietary, while Virginia and Massachusetts became royal.

questions.q: Leisler's Rebellion (1689-1691) in New York was fueled by what?
options: A dispute over tobacco prices and the shipping fees charged by planters
A Native uprising
A fight over slavery
Resentment of elite control and fear of Catholic rule after the Glorious Revolution
questions.explain: Jacob Leisler, a merchant, seized control of New York, claiming to defend Protestantism, but was executed after royal officials regained control.

questions.q: Which was the largest city in the British colonies by the 1750s?
options: Philadelphia
Charles Town
Boston
Williamsburg
questions.explain: Philadelphia's grain trade and welcoming policies helped it overtake Boston by the 1750s, making it the largest city and busiest port in British America.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin founded the Library Company of Philadelphia in 1731 as what?
options: A school that trained young sailors and ship captains in navigation and trade
A printing business
A subscription library that shared books among members
A museum of science
questions.explain: Members pooled money to buy books, an example of Enlightenment-era civic improvement and the spread of learning.

questions.q: What made the almanac Franklin published under the name Richard Saunders so popular with colonial readers?
options: It listed the king's laws and royal proclamations for each year in order
It combined practical information with witty sayings promoting thrift and hard work
It taught Latin
It printed sermons
questions.explain: Sayings like "A penny saved is two pence clear" reflected, and shaped, values of thrift associated with the middle colonies and later American culture.

questions.q: Franklin's experiments with electricity in the 1740s and 1750s are often cited as an example of what?
options: The continued influence of Puritan theology on scientific research in the colonies
Spanish exploration
Native knowledge
The influence of Enlightenment science in the colonies
questions.explain: Franklin's reputation in Europe grew as colonists took part in the transatlantic scientific community.

questions.q: Which colonial city's newspaper, the Boston News-Letter (1704), was notable as what?
options: The first newspaper in the colonies to criticize the king by name in print
The first continuously published newspaper in the colonies
A Native newspaper
A French-language paper
questions.explain: Newspapers expanded access to information, and later colonists used them to spread political ideas.

questions.q: John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) argued that government exists to protect which rights?
options: Life, liberty, and property
Divine right of kings
Church control
Hereditary titles
questions.explain: Locke's ideas of natural rights and consent of the governed influenced colonial thought and later documents like the Declaration of Independence.

questions.q: Locke's idea of a 'social contract' held that what?
options: Kings rule by divine right and are answerable to God rather than to their subjects
Government is unnecessary
Government's authority comes from the consent of the governed
The church should govern
questions.explain: If rulers violated people's natural rights, Locke argued, people had the right to alter or replace them.

questions.q: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement that emphasized what?
options: Strict obedience to church authority and acceptance of religious tradition
Rejection of learning
Support for absolute monarchy
Reason, science, and the questioning of traditional authority
questions.explain: Thinkers like Newton and Locke inspired colonists to apply reason to politics, religion, and nature.

questions.q: Deism, popular among some Enlightenment-influenced colonists, held that what?
options: God directly controls every event and answers prayer through daily miracles
There is no God
God created the universe but does not intervene in daily affairs
Salvation depends on a church
questions.explain: Deists such as Franklin valued reason over revelation and generally supported religious tolerance.

questions.q: How did the Enlightenment and the Great Awakening differ in emphasis?
options: Both rejected religion
The Enlightenment stressed reason, while the Awakening stressed emotion and personal faith
Both stressed obedience to the Crown
The Enlightenment stressed emotional conversion, while the Awakening stressed scientific reasoning
questions.explain: Both movements, however, challenged established authority and encouraged individuals to think for themselves.

questions.q: The Molasses Act of 1733 imposed high duties on molasses imported from which source?
options: Non-British colonies in the West Indies
British colonies in the West Indies
Spain only
Virginia
questions.explain: Colonists often ignored the law by smuggling, which illustrates the weak enforcement of salutary neglect.

questions.q: The Hat Act of 1732 and the Iron Act of 1750 were passed to do what?
options: Raise money to pay for the defense of Native allies against French attacks
Encourage colonial growth
Limit colonial manufacturing that competed with English industries
Increase imports from France
questions.explain: These mercantilist laws sought to keep the colonies as suppliers of raw materials and consumers of English goods.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how mercantilism affected colonial economies?
options: Colonies were encouraged to build factories
Colonies were expected to supply raw materials and buy manufactured goods from England
Colonies were free to trade with any nation they chose
Colonies were self-sufficient
questions.explain: Trade rules benefited English merchants, but colonists also profited from a protected imperial market and shipping.

questions.q: How did colonists often respond to trade restrictions they disliked?
options: By smuggling goods or ignoring the rules
By declaring war on the Royal Navy and seizing English trading ships at sea
By leaving the colonies
By petitioning Spain
questions.explain: Because enforcement was lax, smuggling was common, especially of molasses and other goods.

questions.q: Which statement best describes colonial population growth between 1700 and 1750?
options: It declined sharply because of epidemic disease and a lack of new migrants
It stayed constant
It rose only in the North
It rose rapidly because of natural increase and immigration
questions.explain: Plentiful land, early marriage, and migration from Europe and Africa meant the population multiplied several times.

questions.q: Population growth in the 1700s increased demand for what, leading to westward expansion?
options: Fish
Land
Spanish gold
Imported silk
questions.explain: Colonists pushed into the backcountry, creating conflicts with Native nations and with France.

questions.q: Which colleges were established in the colonies in the 1700s, partly as a result of the Great Awakening?
options: Princeton and Brown
Harvard and Yale
Notre Dame and Georgetown
MIT and Johns Hopkins
questions.explain: New Light revivalists founded colleges like Princeton (1746) and Brown (1764) to train ministers sympathetic to the Awakening.

questions.q: William and Mary, founded in 1693, was the second college in the colonies and was established in which colony?
options: Maryland
Pennsylvania
Virginia
Georgia
questions.explain: The Anglican college trained clergy and sons of the gentry, including future leaders like Thomas Jefferson.

questions.q: Which statement best describes colonial education in the 1700s?
options: It was run entirely by the Crown through schools in each royal colony
It was universal and free
It was banned in the South
It was left to families, churches, and local communities, with the strongest public effort in New England
questions.explain: Literacy was highest in New England, where laws encouraged schools, and lowest in many southern areas with dispersed populations.

questions.q: Compared with plantation colonies, the economies of the middle colonies were more what?
options: Dependent mainly on a single cash crop exported to England each year
Based on mining
Diversified, combining grain farming, trade, and small manufacturing
Controlled by the Crown
questions.explain: Farms, mills, ironworks, and commerce gave the region a varied economy.

questions.q: Which colony's iron industry was notable in the 1700s despite English restrictions?
options: Georgia
New Hampshire
South Carolina
Pennsylvania
questions.explain: Iron furnaces in the Pennsylvania countryside supplied tools and goods for the colonies.

questions.q: Which statement best describes slavery in the northern colonies in the 1700s?
options: Slavery was illegal in every northern colony by the early 1700s
Enslaved people worked as household servants, artisans, and farmhands, especially in cities such as New York
Slavery was concentrated on large plantations
Slavery did not exist
questions.explain: Slavery was legal in nearly every colony for most of the 1700s (Georgia banned it from 1735 to 1751), but the largest concentrations were in the South.

questions.q: Pennsylvania's treatment of religious diversity in the early 1700s helped attract immigrants because it offered what?
options: Religious toleration and a government that protected liberties
A state church supported by taxes, as in Massachusetts and Virginia
Free land for Catholics
A ban on Quakers
questions.explain: This reputation drew Germans, Scots-Irish, and others who sought freedom to worship.

questions.q: The 1670s English Plantation Duty Act imposed a tax on what?
options: Enumerated goods shipped from one colony to another
Imports of manufactured goods from Spain and the Spanish colonies
Imports of slaves
Exports of fish
questions.explain: The 1673 law aimed to stop colonists from evading the enumeration rules by moving goods to other colonies.

questions.q: Which ruler took the English throne after the Restoration in 1660?
options: Oliver Cromwell
James I
Charles II
George III
questions.explain: Charles II rewarded supporters with colonial charters, creating colonies like Carolina, New York, and Pennsylvania.

questions.q: Many English colonies founded after 1660, such as Carolina, New York, and Pennsylvania, are known as what?
options: Reformation colonies
Puritan colonies
Royal fortresses
Restoration colonies
questions.explain: Charles II granted these territories to loyal supporters, mostly as proprietary colonies.

questions.q: Which colony was granted in 1663 to eight Lords Proprietors and later divided into North and South?
options: Georgia
Carolina
Maryland
Delaware
questions.explain: The proprietors hoped to profit from land and trade, and the colonies later became royal colonies in 1729.

questions.q: Which of these best describes the 'rights of Englishmen' that colonists claimed?
options: Rights granted to colonists by the Spanish crown in the Treaty of Tordesillas
Rights to hold slaves only
Rights to vote for the Parliament
Traditional liberties such as trial by jury and no taxation without representation by their own assemblies
questions.explain: Colonists saw themselves as inheritors of English liberties dating back to Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights of 1689.

questions.q: Which English document of 1689 limited royal power and protected certain rights?
options: The English Bill of Rights
The Magna Carta
The Mayflower Compact
The Albany Plan
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights, passed after the Glorious Revolution, affirmed Parliament's authority and barred cruel punishments and unlawful taxation by the king.

questions.q: The Magna Carta (1215) influenced colonial political thought by establishing what idea?
options: That the king is divine
That even a king must obey the law
That Parliament must be abolished
That all men can vote
questions.explain: Colonists often cited this tradition when arguing that governments must respect established rights.

questions.q: The Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s was a movement that emphasized what?
options: Strict obedience to royal bishops and the established church hierarchy
Rational study of nature only
Emotional, personal religious experience and conversion
Rejection of Christianity
questions.explain: Revival preachers urged listeners to experience a spiritual rebirth rather than rely on church membership alone.

questions.q: Jonathan Edwards's 1741 sermon 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' aimed to do what?
options: Support English rule by teaching colonists to obey the Crown and its governors
Teach navigation
Reject predestination
Convince listeners of their need for salvation by describing God's judgment
questions.explain: Edwards's vivid imagery of hell stirred emotional reactions and fueled revivals in New England.

questions.q: George Whitefield, an English minister, became famous in the colonies during the 1740s for what?
options: Preaching to huge outdoor crowds with a dramatic style
Founding Harvard College and writing the first laws on education for the colony
Commanding a militia
Writing the Mayflower Compact
questions.explain: His tours up and down the coast made him one of the first intercolonial celebrities and helped unite colonists in a common experience.

questions.q: Revivalists were called 'New Lights,' while those who opposed the emotional style of the Awakening were called what?
options: Dim Lights
Sons of Liberty
Old Lights
Separatists
questions.explain: Old Lights, often established ministers, objected to emotional preaching and itinerant ministers who challenged settled clergy.

questions.q: One political effect of the Great Awakening was that it did what?
options: Strengthened the Church of England and the established authority of bishops in the colonies
Encouraged colonists to question established authority, religious and civil
Ended religious diversity
Supported royal authority
questions.explain: Because individuals judged preachers themselves, deference to elites eroded, a habit that would matter in later political disputes.

questions.q: The Great Awakening is sometimes called the first major event shared by colonists across regions because it did what?
options: Created a single colonial government that united the colonies under one leader
Ended slavery
Established an American church
Reached many colonies through traveling preachers and printed sermons
questions.explain: Revivals spanned New England to Georgia, giving colonists a sense of common experience beyond their separate colonies.

questions.q: How did the Great Awakening affect some enslaved Africans and Native peoples?
options: It forbade their conversion and urged ministers to avoid preaching to them
It brought many to Christianity as preachers welcomed them
It freed them
It banned church attendance
questions.explain: Evangelical preaching, which stressed spiritual equality, led some enslaved people to embrace Christianity, though slaveholders often used religion to justify control.

questions.q: Which religious groups grew in numbers during and after the Great Awakening?
options: Baptists and Presbyterians
Anglicans only
Puritan Congregationalists only
Catholics
questions.explain: New denominations gained followers in the South and backcountry, challenging the Anglican establishment.

questions.q: Which Mohegan minister became well known for his preaching during and after the Awakening?
options: Metacom
Pontiac
Samson Occom
Squanto
questions.explain: Occom, educated by a New Light minister, became an ordained Presbyterian and an author, showing Native engagement with Christianity on their own terms.

questions.q: Which argument did Old Lights make against itinerant preachers?
options: They were too highly educated and spoke over the heads of ordinary listeners
They spoke Spanish
They opposed religion
They disrupted order and undermined the authority of settled ministers
questions.explain: Traditional ministers resented traveling preachers who criticized them as unconverted.

questions.q: The Great Awakening's emphasis on personal religious decision had what lasting cultural impact?
options: It ended all religious disputes by uniting the colonists in a single church
It created one national church
It encouraged a belief in individual judgment that helped shape American religion
It made ministers royal officials
questions.explain: Competing denominations and voluntary religion became a feature of American life.

questions.q: In the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Pueblo peoples in New Mexico did what?
options: Drove the Spanish out of the province
Joined the Spanish army and fought together with them against the Apache
Moved to Florida
Signed a treaty with France
questions.explain: Led by a religious leader named Popé, the Pueblo coordinated an uprising that forced Spanish settlers to retreat to present-day El Paso region.

questions.q: Which factor helped cause the Pueblo Revolt of 1680?
options: A war with the French over the control of the fur trade in the north
Spanish suppression of Native religion and forced labor demands
Taxes imposed by Parliament
A dispute over tobacco
questions.explain: Friars attacked Pueblo ceremonies, and the encomienda and tribute demands, along with drought and disease, pushed many to rebel.

questions.q: After the Spanish returned to New Mexico in the 1690s, what changed in colonial policy?
options: They ended all missions and moved the Pueblo to new towns far from the Rio Grande
They granted independence
Spanish officials generally tolerated some Pueblo religious practices and used less harsh labor demands
They banned Spanish settlers
questions.explain: The revolt forced a more accommodating approach, and the Pueblo and Spanish developed a more mixed coexistence.

questions.q: Which statement describes the long-term effect of the Pueblo Revolt on the Southwest?
options: It ended Spanish settlement forever and left the region without any European rule
It helped spread horses to other Native peoples
It created an English colony
It established a French fort
questions.explain: Horses taken or traded from Spanish herds moved onto the Plains and changed the lives of groups such as the Comanche, though scholars note horses spread by several routes.

questions.q: Santa Fe, founded about 1610, served as what for Spain?
options: A French fort built to protect the Mississippi River trade from English raiders
An English trading post
A Dutch settlement
The capital of the province of New Mexico
questions.explain: Spain built Santa Fe as an administrative and religious center, and it remains one of the oldest state capitals in the United States.

questions.q: Spain established missions in Texas, such as San Antonio de Valero in 1718, mainly to do what?
options: Counter French expansion from Louisiana and convert Native peoples
Support English settlers moving south from Virginia into Spanish territory
Mine gold
Trade with the Dutch
questions.explain: The Spanish worried about French moves from Louisiana and used missions and presidios to claim territory.

questions.q: Which French explorer claimed the Mississippi River valley for France in 1682 and named it Louisiana?
options: Samuel de Champlain
Jacques Cartier
Robert de La Salle
Louis Joliet
questions.explain: La Salle named the territory for King Louis XIV, giving France a vast claim stretching from Canada to the Gulf.

questions.q: Which city, founded by the French in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi, became a major port?
options: Charleston
Mobile
Savannah
New Orleans
questions.explain: Founded by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, the city controlled access to the river and the Gulf.

questions.q: French colonists in North America known as coureurs de bois were most concerned with what?
options: Trading furs and building alliances with Native peoples
Developing large plantations worked by enslaved people along the Mississippi
Silver mining
Religious dissent
questions.explain: The fur trade drew French traders deep into the interior, and they often adopted Native customs and married into Native communities.

questions.q: Why was New France's population much smaller than that of the English colonies by 1750?
options: Spain controlled the St. Lawrence valley and kept the French out
France encouraged fewer settlers and focused on trade rather than farming settlements
It was too warm
Native peoples blocked all settlement
questions.explain: Roughly 60,000 French colonists lived in New France compared with more than a million in British America.

questions.q: The Haudenosaunee kept a policy of neutrality between France and Britain in the early 1700s because it let them do what?
options: Stay out of all trade with Europeans to avoid dependence on foreign goods
Protect their independence and gain trade advantages from both sides
Give up land
Join the Spanish
questions.explain: By playing European powers against each other, the League retained power during a period of colonial rivalry.

questions.q: The Covenant Chain was a diplomatic alliance linking which groups?
options: The Haudenosaunee and the English colonies
The French and the Huron, who joined together against the English colonies
The Spanish and the Pueblo
The Dutch and the Powhatan
questions.explain: The chain symbolized an alliance in which the Haudenosaunee served as intermediaries with other Native nations and strengthened the English position against France.

questions.q: The Beaver Wars of the 1600s were conflicts in which the Haudenosaunee fought neighbors over what?
options: Religious teaching and the conversion of Native peoples to Christianity
Spanish gold
Control of the fur trade and access to hunting territories
Tobacco land
questions.explain: Armed with Dutch and English guns, the Haudenosaunee expanded their power against the Huron and others.

questions.q: Queen Anne's War (1702-1713) ended with the Treaty of Utrecht, which gave Britain what?
options: Control of Louisiana and the Mississippi River from the French crown
Florida
Quebec
Control of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia (Acadia), and Hudson Bay
questions.explain: The treaty strengthened Britain in North America and also gave it the right to sell enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies (the asiento).

questions.q: King George's War (1744-1748) saw New England forces capture which French fortress, which was returned at the war's end?
options: Quebec
Fort Duquesne
Montreal
Louisbourg
questions.explain: The return of Louisbourg to France in 1748 angered many New Englanders who had fought for it.

questions.q: Which factor made the Ohio River valley a focus of French and British rivalry in the 1740s and 1750s?
options: Large deposits of gold and silver that both empires wanted to mine
Fertile land and fur trade connections attracting both empires
The Pacific shipping route
Spanish settlements
questions.explain: British traders and land companies pushed west while France sought to link Canada and Louisiana.

questions.q: In 1753, Virginia's governor sent a young George Washington to deliver a message to French forces in the Ohio country. What was the message?
options: An offer to trade with the French in return for Virginia's western land claims
A declaration of independence
A demand that the French leave land claimed by Britain
A request for help against Spain
questions.explain: Washington's journey and his later skirmishes there helped set off the French and Indian War.

questions.q: Fort Necessity, where a young George Washington surrendered to French forces in 1754, was built in which area?
options: Western Pennsylvania, near the Ohio country
The harbor of Boston, in the colony of Massachusetts Bay
Charleston
Quebec
questions.explain: The defeat and Washington's earlier attack on a French party in 1754 marked the start of the war that decided control of eastern North America.

questions.q: The Albany Congress of 1754 brought together colonial delegates to do what?
options: Declare independence from the British Crown and form a new national government
Discuss cooperation in defense and relations with the Haudenosaunee
Write the Constitution
Vote on slavery
questions.explain: Delegates met as war with France loomed and considered a proposal for colonial unity.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin's Albany Plan of Union (1754) proposed what?
options: Independence from Britain and a written constitution for the thirteen colonies
A Native confederacy
A central council and a president-general for the colonies' defense and Native affairs
Abolishing the colonial assemblies
questions.explain: Colonial assemblies and the Crown rejected the plan, but it showed an early idea of union among the colonies.

questions.q: Franklin's 1754 cartoon 'Join, or Die,' showing a snake cut into pieces, was meant to do what?
options: Urge colonies to unite against threats
Support the Crown by encouraging the colonists to obey royal governors
Celebrate victory
Mock Native peoples
questions.explain: The image became a famous symbol of colonial unity and was reused during the later Revolutionary era.

questions.q: Why did many Native nations ally with France rather than Britain in the 1750s?
options: The French offered citizenship and land grants to every Native nation that joined them
Britain had no goods
France paid higher taxes
France's presence relied on trade and did not threaten Native land as much as British settlement
questions.explain: The prospect of expanding British farms in the Ohio country alarmed Native nations in the region.

questions.q: During the wars between Britain and France, Native nations often did what?
options: Followed European orders and fought wherever colonial governors sent them
Stayed neutral permanently
Never fought
Pursued their own interests, choosing alliances that protected their land and trade
questions.explain: Native leaders were diplomats who used European rivalry to secure their position rather than passive pawns.

questions.q: The Treaty of Utrecht (1713) included the asiento, which gave Britain the right to do what?
options: Claim Louisiana and the Mississippi River for the British crown
Trade tobacco to France
Supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies
Settle Florida
questions.explain: The contract shows how Atlantic empires competed for control of the slave trade, which was among the most profitable.

questions.q: Which statement best describes how the Spanish in Florida treated escaped enslaved people from the English colonies in the early 1700s?
options: They returned the fugitives to their English owners in exchange for ransom payments
They offered freedom to those who converted to Catholicism and served Spain
They enslaved them
They ignored them
questions.explain: This policy was partly religious and partly strategic, aimed at weakening the English colonies.

questions.q: In 1688, a group of Quakers in Germantown, Pennsylvania, issued a protest against slavery. Why is this significant?
options: It was one of the first public antislavery statements in the colonies
It ended slavery in Pennsylvania and led the colony to free its enslaved residents
It was written by King William
It supported slave trading
questions.explain: The petition argued that slavery violated the Golden Rule, but the Quaker community took decades to turn the idea into action.

questions.q: Samuel Sewall's 1700 pamphlet 'The Selling of Joseph' is known as what?
options: A defense of slavery based on Scripture, written by a Massachusetts minister
A guide to farming
A treaty with Native peoples
An early antislavery tract in New England
questions.explain: A Massachusetts judge who had taken part in the Salem trials, Sewall argued that slavery contradicted Christian teaching.

questions.q: During Boston's 1721 smallpox epidemic, Cotton Mather and Zabdiel Boylston promoted inoculation. Mather learned of the practice from whom?
options: Onesimus, an enslaved African man in his household
A Native healer from the Wampanoag nation who was known in the Boston area
A French doctor
A Dutch sailor
questions.explain: Onesimus described inoculation as practiced in West Africa, an example of African knowledge contributing to colonial medicine.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the religious beliefs of enslaved Africans in colonial America?
options: They adopted only Puritan practices and gave up every African religious tradition
They had no religion
They blended African traditions with Christianity, creating distinctive forms of worship
They followed only Islam
questions.explain: Enslaved communities preserved aspects of African spirituality, music, and storytelling while also adopting Christian elements.

questions.q: What was the Atlantic slave trade's effect on West Africa?
options: It enriched all African societies and ended warfare along the coast
It disrupted societies and increased violence and warfare to capture people
It ended African trade
It strengthened family life
questions.explain: Millions were taken from regions across West and Central Africa, and the trade encouraged some states to raid neighbors.

questions.q: Most Africans taken across the Atlantic in the slave trade were sent to which regions?
options: The mainland colonies of North America, such as Virginia and South Carolina
Europe
Brazil and the Caribbean
The Pacific
