questions.explain: Only a small share of the roughly 12 million embarked arrived in what became the United States; most went to sugar colonies.

questions.q: By 1750, about what share of the population of the British mainland colonies was of African descent?
options: About one in five
Nearly half
About one in fifty
About three in four
questions.explain: The population was concentrated in the Chesapeake and Lowcountry, where enslaved people made up a large share.

questions.q: Louisiana's 1724 Code Noir, issued by France, did what?
options: Abolished slavery in Louisiana and freed all enslaved people who were baptized
Regulated slavery and required enslaved people be baptized as Catholics
Gave voting rights
Banned the slave trade
questions.explain: The code gave owners power but also set some limits, and it reflected France's attempt to regulate its colonial slave society.

questions.q: The term 'seasoning' referred to what in early southern colonies?
options: The harvest season when workers brought in tobacco and rice for sale
A religious ceremony
A trading season
The period when newly arrived people were exposed to disease and adapted to the climate
questions.explain: Many newcomers, European and African, died within a few years of arrival from disease.

questions.q: Margaret Brent, a landowner in Maryland, in 1648 asked the colonial assembly for what?
options: A reduction in taxes
A new charter
Land from Native peoples
A vote in the assembly
questions.explain: Her request was refused, but it shows that women with property sometimes tried to claim political rights.

questions.q: Colonial apprenticeship was a system in which young people did what?
options: Studied at a college to prepare for the ministry or the practice of law
Joined the militia
Learned a trade by working for a master for a number of years
Worked in plantations only
questions.explain: Apprentices received training and room and board, and the system shaped urban crafts and families.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the colonial concept of 'deference'?
options: Ordinary people were expected to respect the authority of the wealthy and educated elite
Everyone had an equal voice in politics regardless of wealth or social rank
The king had no power
Ministers were disliked
questions.explain: Deference shaped politics and social life, though the Great Awakening and later events weakened it.

questions.q: Which activity was most important to the economy of the Chesapeake in the 1700s?
options: Fur trading
Exporting tobacco to Europe
Textile manufacturing
Whaling
questions.explain: Tobacco was Virginia's and Maryland's main export, driving the plantation system.

questions.q: Whaling and shipbuilding were important in which colonial region?
options: New England
Georgia
The Carolinas
The backcountry
questions.explain: Harbors, forests, and the Atlantic gave New Englanders resources for maritime industries.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a colonial region with its main economic basis?
options: The Lowcountry, whaling; the Chesapeake, rice
New England, rice; the middle colonies, tobacco
The middle colonies, sugar; the Lowcountry, furs
The Chesapeake, tobacco; New England, trade and fishing
questions.explain: Regional environments shaped different economic systems, from plantation staples in the South to commerce in the North.

questions.q: The Appalachian Mountains acted as a barrier that did what in the colonial period?
options: Prevented all trade
Slowed British settlement into the interior
Protected Native lands permanently
Divided the colonies into two nations
questions.explain: Most colonists lived east of the mountains until the mid-1700s, and conflicts arose as farmers moved west.

questions.q: In the colonial period, roads were poor and most long-distance trade moved by what means?
options: Railroads running between the colonial capitals and the main ports
Rivers and the Atlantic coast
Canals
Air travel
questions.explain: Waterways connected plantations and ports, so coastal and river towns were centers of trade.

questions.q: French Protestants known as Huguenots who settled in colonies such as South Carolina and New York were fleeing what?
options: A famine that had struck the French countryside after several poor harvests
Spanish invasion
Religious persecution in France
Plague
questions.explain: King Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 led many to flee France.

questions.q: Jewish refugees arrived in New Amsterdam in 1654. What did Governor Peter Stuyvesant want to do?
options: Welcome them and offer land grants and tax exemptions to the families
Give them land
Make them governors
Prevent them from staying, but the Dutch West India Company overruled him
questions.explain: The company's investors, including Jewish shareholders, overruled him, allowing the group to remain.

questions.q: Which factor most encouraged religious diversity in the middle colonies?
options: Proprietors who valued toleration to attract settlers
Strict laws against dissent that banned most religions other than the established church
Establishment of Puritanism
Spanish influence
questions.explain: Commercial and philosophical motives led New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania to accept many faiths.

questions.q: In colonial America, an indentured servant who completed a contract usually received what, called 'freedom dues'?
options: A government salary paid by the colony for each year of service
A title
Tools, clothing, or sometimes land
A trade license
questions.explain: The payment helped start independent life, though many former servants struggled to obtain land.

questions.q: Which was a likely reason colonial legislatures grew more assertive in the 1700s?
options: The king moved to America and ruled directly from the colonial capitals
Parliament abolished them
They were controlled by Native leaders
Local elites gained experience and distance from London limited oversight
questions.explain: Distance and the importance of colonial taxes meant assemblies often won disputes with governors.

questions.q: Which Spanish colony in the southeast did the English target in raids around 1702 to 1704?
options: Texas
Florida
California
Louisiana
questions.explain: Carolina forces under James Moore attacked Spanish missions and Native allies, devastating the Spanish mission system.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Spanish mission system in Florida by the early 1700s?
options: It grew stronger as English raids forced Native peoples to seek missionary protection
It was taken by the Dutch
It was largely destroyed by English and Native raids from Carolina
It became Protestant
questions.explain: The collapse of missions, combined with disease and the Indian slave trade, devastated Native communities in Florida.

questions.q: The Southeast deerskin trade, in which Cherokee, Creek, and Choctaw hunters exchanged skins for European goods, did what?
options: Linked Native economies to Atlantic markets and created dependence on trade goods
Ended Native farming and led most Native peoples to stop growing crops
Gave Native peoples control of Europe
Was banned
questions.explain: Hunters exchanged skins for guns, cloth, and metal tools, and debts to traders sometimes sparked conflict.

questions.q: How did Native peoples in the Southeast, such as the Creek, handle competition between Spain, France, and England?
options: Served as soldiers in every European army that came to the Southeast
Used diplomacy to balance one power against another
Left the region
Accepted one empire's rule permanently
questions.explain: Creek leaders traded with all three powers, aiming to keep their independence.

questions.q: Which colonial figure and printer helped create a postal and communication network, strengthening links among colonies?
options: Benjamin Franklin
John Hancock
Patrick Henry
Roger Williams
questions.explain: Franklin served as colonial deputy postmaster, improving mail delivery and the exchange of news among colonies.

questions.q: George Washington was born in 1732 into a family that held land in which colony?
options: Maryland
Pennsylvania
Virginia
Massachusetts
questions.explain: He was born in Westmoreland County, Virginia, into a family of tobacco planters that owned enslaved workers.

questions.q: As a teenager in the late 1740s, Washington gained early experience working as what?
options: A land surveyor in Virginia's backcountry
A ship's navigator in Boston
A fur trader in New York
A printer's apprentice in Philadelphia
questions.explain: Surveying for the powerful Fairfax family introduced him to western lands, a topic that later tied his career to the Ohio country.

questions.q: Washington's 1754 expedition into the Ohio country, which ended at Fort Necessity, was sent by whom?
options: King George II, who personally selected Washington for the mission
The Massachusetts legislature
The Continental Congress
Virginia's colonial governor, Robert Dinwiddie
questions.explain: Dinwiddie wanted to protect Virginia investors' claims against French forts; the clash helped trigger the French and Indian War.

questions.q: The Ohio Company of Virginia, formed in 1747, sought to profit mainly from what?
options: Whaling off the New England coast and selling the oil to London merchants
Settling and trading on western lands claimed by Virginia
Mining silver in Mexico
Exporting rice from Charles Town
questions.explain: Investors, including members of Washington's family, received a royal land grant near the Forks of the Ohio, which collided with French plans.

questions.q: Why did colonial leaders in Virginia like Washington care about the 'Forks of the Ohio' where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet?
options: It was the capital of Virginia and the seat of the royal governor
It was the site of a gold mine
It was the only route to the Pacific
Control of that spot would give access to river routes and western trade
questions.explain: The Forks later held Fort Duquesne and then Fort Pitt, showing the importance of waterways for travel and trade.

questions.q: Which statement about the French and Indian War's start is most accurate?
options: A Spanish fleet attacked Charles Town and drew the colonies into a war with Spain
A Virginia-led expedition in the Ohio country triggered fighting before war was formally declared
Parliament declared war after a Boston protest
A Native alliance invaded Williamsburg
questions.explain: Fighting between Washington's men and French troops in 1754 began a conflict that became a global war by 1756.

questions.q: What did Virginia planters like Washington's family typically use to pay British merchants for goods?
options: Gold bars mined in the colony and shipped to English merchants
Wheat shipped to Spain
Tobacco shipped to England on credit accounts
Furs traded with France
questions.explain: Because tobacco was the main export, planters often kept debt accounts with London merchants, tying them to the empire's economy.

questions.q: Which English scientist's laws of motion convinced many Enlightenment thinkers that the universe followed rational laws?
options: Isaac Newton
Francis Drake
Thomas Hobbes
William Harvey
questions.explain: Newton's Principia (1687) inspired the hope that reason could uncover natural laws in politics and society too.

questions.q: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) influenced colonial thinkers by promoting which idea?
options: Rule by a single hereditary king advised by a council of nobles
A single legislature with unlimited power
Separating government powers among different branches
Church control of laws
questions.explain: His argument that dividing power protects liberty later shaped how Americans designed their state and national governments.

questions.q: Which colony's early experiment with religious freedom, begun by Roger Williams, is often cited as a precedent for the later idea of separating church and state?
options: Virginia
Massachusetts Bay
New Haven
Rhode Island
questions.explain: Williams argued that government should not control belief, and Rhode Island's example later fed arguments like Jefferson's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom.

questions.q: Colonial elites like Thomas Jefferson attended the College of William and Mary partly because it offered what?
options: Training for Catholic priests and missionaries to the Native peoples of the region
Education in law, science, and classics for Virginia's gentry
Preparation for the fur trade
A degree needed to vote
questions.explain: The Anglican college in Williamsburg educated many of Virginia's future political leaders, including Jefferson.

questions.q: Colonial Deists such as Franklin tended to say that people should judge religion mostly by what?
options: Priestly authority
Tradition alone
Royal decree
Reason and moral conduct
questions.explain: Deism downplayed dramatic revelation and emphasized a rational, tolerant approach to belief.

questions.q: A colonial pamphlet in 1740 argues that rulers earn obedience only by protecting citizens' rights. Which thinker's ideas most directly shaped this argument?
options: Thomas Aquinas
King James I
John Locke
Niccolo Machiavelli
questions.explain: Locke's theory that government rests on consent and protects natural rights circulated widely in colonial newspapers and sermons.

questions.q: Which colony was unusual for having only one legislative house after 1701?
options: Virginia
New York
South Carolina
Pennsylvania
questions.explain: Pennsylvania's Charter of Privileges created a single elected assembly, unlike the two-house legislatures of most other colonies.

questions.q: A royal governor's veto power over colonial laws meant that he could do what?
options: Block a bill passed by the colonial legislature
Dissolve the king's Parliament in London when it voted for new taxes
Appoint Native chiefs
Set prices for crops
questions.explain: Governors often clashed with assemblies, and colonists later pointed to such executive powers when criticizing British rule.

questions.q: Why did colonial legislatures sometimes withhold a governor's salary?
options: To save money for churches
To pressure him into accepting laws the assembly wanted
To pay for Native treaties
Because the governor was elected by the assembly
questions.explain: Control of the purse gave assemblies influence over royal appointees who depended on their pay.

questions.q: The Privy Council in London could do what to a law passed by a colonial legislature?
options: Rewrite it to suit colonial voters
Send it to Native leaders
Disallow it, overturning the law
Enforce it without the governor
questions.explain: This power of review linked the colonies to royal authority, though it was used sparingly.

questions.q: Which of the following was a typical power of a colonial governor in a royal colony?
options: Choosing church ministers and deciding the doctrines taught in parishes
Appointing judges and calling or dismissing the assembly
Electing the council
Setting Parliament's agenda
questions.explain: Royal governors held large executive authority, but assemblies' control over taxation limited it.

questions.q: What was a major reason Maryland and Pennsylvania remained proprietary colonies into the 1700s?
options: Founding families kept charter rights to appoint officials and receive land revenue
The king did not want to give up his claim to the colonies' land revenue
They had no legislatures
Native peoples owned them
questions.explain: Proprietors such as the Calverts and Penns held rights to govern and sell land, though assemblies challenged their authority.

questions.q: When the Virginia General Assembly first met in 1619, burgesses were representatives from what units?
options: Native villages that had signed treaties of alliance with the Virginia Company
Royal forts
Church parishes only in London
Plantations and settlements across the colony
questions.explain: Each community sent two representatives to Jamestown to help make laws and set taxes with the governor.

questions.q: The Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) is notable for what?
options: Banning all forms of religion except the church of the Puritans
Giving the king new powers
Ending the General Court
Listing rights that protected colonists from arbitrary punishment
questions.explain: This early legal code included protections such as a limit on double punishment for the same offense, a forerunner of later rights.

questions.q: The 1606 charter that created the Virginia Company promised colonists what legal assurance?
options: That they would be free from all laws
That they could own Native land by purchase
That they would keep the rights of English subjects
That Parliament would never tax them
questions.explain: This promise of English liberties became a foundation for colonists' later claims against British policy.

questions.q: In colonial town meetings, a free adult man might help decide which of the following?
options: Local taxes, roads, and the election of town officers
The war plans of the king and the terms of royal treaties with Native peoples
The choice of the governor
The appointment of bishops for the colony
questions.explain: These meetings gave many New England men direct experience in self-government.

questions.q: Colonial assemblies were modeled most closely on which part of the English Parliament?
options: The Privy Council
The House of Commons
The House of Lords
The Court of Star Chamber
questions.explain: Colonists saw their assemblies as like the Commons, with the power to approve taxes.

questions.q: Roger Williams wrote that a 'wall of separation' should exist between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world. This idea later influenced which American principle?
options: Unlimited royal power
Taxation without representation
Federal supremacy
Separation of church and state
questions.explain: Williams's phrase, from the 1640s, is often cited as an early source of the idea behind the First Amendment's religion clauses.

questions.q: The writ of habeas corpus, protected by an English law of 1679, guards against what?
options: Being jailed without being told the legal reason
Paying taxes to a government in which one has no elected representatives
Being forced to attend church
Having property seized by pirates
questions.explain: Colonists saw it as a core English liberty, and the Constitution later restricted when it could be suspended.

questions.q: Colonial courts in New England often punished moral offenses such as drunkenness. This reflects the Puritan idea that law should do what?
options: Treat all personal conduct as a private matter outside the reach of courts
Protect only property
Enforce religious and moral standards in the community
Serve the interests of the king alone
questions.explain: Puritan magistrates saw crime and sin as linked, so courts enforced the covenant community's moral order.

questions.q: English common law, which colonists inherited, relied heavily on what?
options: Written commands issued by the pope and enforced by church courts
Decisions by Native councils
Laws made only by governors
Precedent and traditional rights such as trial by jury
questions.explain: This tradition shaped American courts and fed the claim that colonists possessed 'rights of Englishmen.'

questions.q: The Boston Post Road, established in the 1670s, was important because it did what?
options: Linked Virginia and Georgia for the shipping of tobacco and rice
Connected Boston and New York for mail and travel
Served as a Native trade path to Quebec
Reached the Pacific coast
questions.explain: Riders carried messages along the route, an early step toward a colonial postal network.

questions.q: The Great Wagon Road, used heavily from the 1730s, helped settlers do what?
options: Travel from Pennsylvania down the Shenandoah Valley into the southern backcountry
Cross the Rocky Mountains to reach the Pacific coast and the fur trade
Reach the Mississippi by train
Sail to the West Indies
questions.explain: German and Scots-Irish migrants followed the route south, spreading settlement through the Appalachian valleys.

questions.q: Because land travel was slow and difficult in the colonial era, which transportation method moved most goods between regions?
options: Coastal and river shipping
Railroads that ran between the main colonial ports and the interior
Paved highways
Horse relays only
questions.explain: Ships and boats were cheaper and faster than wagons, which is why ports and rivers shaped where towns grew.

questions.q: Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company in 1609, was searching for what?
options: A Spanish treasure fleet
A sea route to Asia
The Fountain of Youth
A route to Africa
questions.explain: Hired to find a route to Asia, he was blocked by ice in the north, turned west, and explored the river that now bears his name, giving the Dutch a claim in the Hudson valley.

questions.q: Which three ships made up Columbus's first expedition in 1492?
options: The Mayflower, the Speedwell, and the Fortune
The Susan Constant, the Godspeed, and the Discovery
The Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria
The Ark, the Dove, and the Welcome
questions.explain: These small Spanish ships crossed the Atlantic in about five weeks to reach the Bahamas.

questions.q: Which instrument, a magnetized needle that points north, helped European sailors steer when land was out of sight?
options: The sextant
The telescope
The barometer
The compass
questions.explain: Combined with the astrolabe and charts, the compass made long ocean voyages more reliable.

questions.q: Which water route did European explorers hope to find across North America to reach Asia?
options: The Panama Canal
The Northwest Passage
The Suez Canal
The Erie Canal
questions.explain: Cabot, Cartier, Hudson, and others searched for it, mapping northern waters as they went.

questions.q: Samuel de Champlain's maps and journals of New France were valuable because they did what?
options: Mapped Spanish Florida and the missions of the Gulf coast for the French
Showed the Pacific coast
Described the English colonies
Recorded rivers and lakes of the interior for French traders and officials
questions.explain: His explorations of the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes region helped France plan trade routes and alliances.

questions.q: In colonial America, Spanish silver coins known as 'pieces of eight' were widely used because of what?
options: A shortage of English coins in the colonies
A law requiring the colonies to use Spanish coins in all trade
A ban on paper money
Native demand for silver
questions.explain: England restricted exporting coins, so colonists relied on foreign money, including Spanish dollars from trade with the Caribbean.

questions.q: Virginia planters sometimes used receipts for stored tobacco as money, a practice called what?
options: Fiat money
Debt forgiveness
Barter taxes
Commodity money
questions.explain: Tobacco notes circulated like currency, showing how the staple crop shaped the colony's economy.

questions.q: Massachusetts issued some of the first paper money in the colonies in 1690 to do what?
options: Finance the voyage of the Pilgrims and their first winter in Plymouth
Buy land from Native nations
Pay soldiers after a costly military expedition
Replace the Navigation Acts
questions.explain: The bills began as military pay and later became a model for other colonial governments.

questions.q: A tax on goods entering or leaving a port, such as those imposed under the Navigation Acts, is called what?
options: A poll tax
A customs duty
A tithe
An excise on salt
questions.explain: Customs duties raised revenue and shaped trade, and colonists often avoided them by smuggling.

questions.q: English officials argued that the Navigation Acts benefited the empire because they did what?
options: Ended all taxes on trade between England and its colonies
Increased Dutch trade
Raised wages in the colonies
Secured shipping and markets for English merchants and sailors
questions.explain: Mercantilist policy treated trade as a competition among nations, and laws aimed to keep profits within the English empire.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the economic effect of the Navigation Acts on New England shipbuilders?
options: They gained from rules requiring trade to use English or colonial ships
They were banned from trade with England and its colonies altogether
They lost all customers
They had to use Dutch ships
questions.explain: Colonial-built ships counted as English, giving New England yards a protected market.

questions.q: Richard Hakluyt's 1584 Discourse of Western Planting argued that England should do what?
options: End trade with Asia and rely only on goods grown in England itself
Establish colonies in North America to compete with Spain
Join the Spanish empire
Ban overseas voyages
questions.explain: He promoted colonies as a source of raw materials, markets, and strategic advantage, ideas that influenced Raleigh and later Jamestown.

questions.q: Engravings by Theodor de Bry in the 1590s, based on John White's paintings of Roanoke-area Algonquians, mattered because they did what?
options: Showed the English cities that Raleigh's colonists had left behind in 1585
Mapped Spanish forts
Gave European readers vivid images of Native life in North America
Depicted Jamestown's founding
questions.explain: The pictures shaped how Europeans imagined Native peoples, mixing careful observation with European assumptions.

questions.q: James Franklin, Benjamin Franklin's older brother, published the New-England Courant, which became known for doing what?
options: Criticized authorities in print, including over smallpox inoculation
Sold land to settlers and promoted the colony's new towns to English readers
Reported Spanish raids
Taught Latin
questions.explain: The paper was among the first to adopt a bold, critical voice, and the teenage Ben Franklin wrote essays for it.

questions.q: Which Boston printer's 1690 newspaper, Publick Occurrences, was shut down by authorities after a single issue?
options: John Winthrop
Samuel Sewall
Cotton Mather
Benjamin Harris
questions.explain: Officials objected that it lacked a license, showing how colonial governments tried to control what was printed.

questions.q: By the 1660s, laws in Maryland and Virginia were beginning to do what to people of African descent?
options: Guarantee them the right to vote and to hold land in the colony
Define them as enslaved for life rather than as servants for a term
Free them after baptism
Limit owners' powers
questions.explain: These statutes were steps toward a hereditary, race-based slavery that lasted until the Civil War.

questions.q: Which labor system, defined by owners holding people as property for life, grew in English America between the mid-1600s and early 1700s?
options: Indentured servitude
Apprenticeship
Chattel slavery
Sharecropping
questions.explain: Law and custom treated enslaved people as property whose children inherited enslaved status.

questions.q: Which pattern best describes how enslaved families lived in colonial Virginia?
options: All families lived together on the same plantation by colonial law
Families were granted land
Families often lived on different plantations, and sales could separate them
Children went to public school
questions.explain: Owners' control over sales meant separation was a constant threat even as enslaved people built strong family and community ties.

questions.q: Enslaved people in the Chesapeake and Lowcountry preserved African traditions in music, storytelling, and what else?
options: English poetry and the hymns of the Anglican prayer book
Foodways such as okra and rice dishes
Printed newspapers
Royal court dress
questions.explain: Crops and cooking methods from West and Central Africa shaped southern cuisine.

questions.q: Which woman, a Powhatan whose name also appears as Matoaka, married John Rolfe in 1614?
options: Pocahontas
Sacagawea
Malinche
Anne Hutchinson
questions.explain: The marriage was part of a brief peace between the Powhatan and Jamestown colonists.

questions.q: Which Native woman served as interpreter and guide for Hernan Cortes during the conquest of the Aztec Empire?
options: Pocahontas
Malintzin (La Malinche)
Sacagawea
Nanye'hi
questions.explain: Her language skills made her central to Cortes's dealings with Native leaders, though historians view her role in complex ways.

questions.q: Native farmers of the Eastern Woodlands lived mainly in what kind of settlement?
options: Isolated stone castles on hilltops, surrounded by walls and ditches
Floating cities
Tent camps moved weekly
Villages of bark or thatch-covered houses surrounded by fields
questions.explain: Villages of longhouses or wigwams, near rivers and fields, supported seasonal farming, hunting, and fishing.

questions.q: The Haudenosaunee Great Law of Peace is often described as what?
options: A written treaty of alliance signed with the Spanish crown in the 1500s
A written Protestant creed
An oral constitution that joined nations in a league
A trading code for fur
questions.explain: According to tradition, the Peacemaker and Hiawatha united warring nations, and its structure has long drawn scholarly interest.

questions.q: Cortes arrived in Tenochtitlan in 1519 and was received by which Aztec ruler?
options: Moctezuma II
Atahualpa
Pachacuti
Powhatan
questions.explain: The emperor welcomed Cortes into the capital, but tensions led to violence, Moctezuma's death, and the city's fall in 1521.

questions.q: Spanish colonists introduced which animal that became central to ranching and later transformed Native economies in the Southwest?
options: The camel
The bison
The ostrich
The sheep
questions.explain: Navajo people adopted sheep herding and weaving, an example of Native adaptation to Spanish introductions.
